Our cooperation, driven by @POTUS @realDonaldTrump and President @ClaudiaShein, sends criminals a clear message: you will be caught and held accountable. In just one day, U.S. authorities returned three fugitives wanted in Mexico: a member of the CJNG narco-terrorist… pic.twitter.com/DpRj0jxvsd — Embajador Ronald Johnson (@USAmbMex) August 16, 2026

“Our cooperation, driven by @POTUS @realDonaldTrump and President @ClaudiaShein, sends criminals a clear message: you will be caught and held accountable,” he wrote on X.

“In just one day, U.S. authorities returned three fugitives wanted in Mexico: a member of the CJNG narco-terrorist organization wanted on a firearms charge in Guanajuato, a fugitive wanted for murder in Zacatecas, and a third wanted for fraud,” Johnson wrote.

Photographs included in the ambassador’s post showed the fugitives in the custody of U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement. Johnson didn’t say where or when the suspects were detained and handed over to Mexican authorities, and he didn’t identify them by name.

His announcement on Sunday came two months after he said on X that the United States had transferred 313 wanted criminals to Mexico to face justice during President Donald Trump’s second administration. Johnson’s June 15 social media post came almost a month after the Mexican government asserted that the United States hadn’t sent to Mexico any of the 269 people whose extradition it requested between January 2018 and May 2026.

“They haven’t sent anyone,” President Claudia Sheinbaum said on May 19.

She said those people include factureros (fake invoice brokers), ex-governors, people accused of organized crime and people linked to the disappearance of 43 students in Guerrero in 2014.

“There has been no handover of any of these alleged criminals to Mexico,” Sheinbaum said, although in 2022 former Chihuahua governor César Duarte was extradited to Mexico from the U.S. to face corruption charges.

“What does Mexico always ask for? … Reciprocity. Why haven’t they handed anyone over?” asked the president, whose government has sent over 90 organized crime figures to the U.S. in three large transfers that took place in January 2026, August 2025 and February 2025.

U.S. authorities are currently seeking the extradition of Sinaloa Governor Ruben Rocha Moya and other current and former Sinaloa-based officials who U.S. prosecutors accuse of drug trafficking in league with the Sinaloa Cartel. Sheinbaum has endorsed the determination from the FGR and the Ministry of Foreign Affairs that the U.S. Justice Department hasn’t provided sufficient “proof” to establish the probable guilt of Rocha, who is currently on leave, and the other defendants, two of whom turned themselves in to U.S. authorities in May.

With reports from El Financiero

World.title: Opinion: Does it feel safe to go to school in the United States after growing up in Mexico?
World.content:
My first article explored my transition from Mexican schools to American ones.

Today, I want to address the question I am asked most often, having been raised and schooled in Mexico: Is it safe for students to attend school here?

“Attention, this is a lockdown drill. Please remain in your classrooms and lock the doors.” For many students across the United States, these words have become an all-too-familiar refrain.

At my high school in California, lockdown drills are an annoyingly regular part of life, prompted by the grim reality of school shootings. In 2025, the K-12 School Shooting Database Omnilert recorded 233 school shooting incidents, although totals vary significantly depending on how a “school shooting” is defined.

It wasn’t until I moved to California that lockdown drills became a part of my school experience. In Mexico, where I attended school until I was 15, school shootings are practically unheard of. I still remember my first drill, two weeks into sophomore year. I was in English class when an unfamiliar voice blared over the speakers, telling us to turn off the lights, lock the doors and sit silently in the back of the classroom. Confusion was written all over my face, but not because of the drill. When I looked around, everyone else seemed completely unfazed, having seemingly done this hundreds of times before.

After that, I started to notice just how normal it all was. School shootings were mentioned in assemblies, safety procedures were constantly reviewed and we had around five more lockdown drills just that year. Everyone seemed to understand the seriousness of the issue after hearing about it constantly throughout their young lives.

Ironically, when I tell my American friends I grew up in Mexico, their first question is almost always about safety.

Yes, cartels and corruption do exist in Mexico. But no, I have never witnessed a murder, been threatened or traveled to school in a bulletproof car. As a student growing up in San Miguel de Allende, I never faced that kind of danger.

What sets the United States apart (and makes questions about safety in Mexico feel so ironic) is that school shootings are not a predictable kind of danger. They are random, devastating and disturbingly common acts of violence that can shatter the lives of innocent people because of the actions of a single individual.

As a student who attended private, not public, schools in both Mexico and the United States, I recognize that my experience is not the norm. Even so, comparing two similarly resourced educational environments has allowed me to notice clear differences in how school safety is experienced in each country.

My schools here in Mexico were overly cautious, if anything. The bilingual school I attended from fourth through ninth grade, Colegio Newland, had guard dogs protecting the grounds at night and a QR code system for students and adults entering campus each day. I never once felt my safety was threatened at school.

And this focus on safety isn’t limited to the private schools I attended. The Guanajuato Education Ministry provides both public and private schools with protocols for emergencies ranging from evacuations and violence to armed individuals and shootings. Schools are also encouraged to assess risks, create safety plans and regularly practice how to respond.

By contrast, my California boarding school has security guards and locks its front gates at night, but it lacks the advanced measures I grew accustomed to in Mexico. Last year, our classes were even canceled for a day because a neighboring school received a bomb threat. Even so, lockdown drills are routine.

When I lived in Mexico, my friends and I spent most afternoons in the center of San Miguel, getting esquites, papas preparadas, even Starbucks. We stayed out late and would walk home together, yet I never felt unsafe. I used to think that was because I always had my twin brother around, but after moving to the United States, I realized he wasn’t scaring anyone away.

In California, my friends and I spent many weekends in San Francisco. Once, while riding a bus near the Financial District, a fight broke out and quickly became violent. It felt like I was rewatching Fight Club, except there was no Brad Pitt. The people involved kept running on and off the bus, screaming at each other. My friends and I, all international students, watched in horror. But when I looked around, my confusion came back because I noticed the same thing had happened again: everyone else appeared completely unfazed.

Danger should never feel normal, yet the nonchalance of my classmates and the people on that bus made me realize just how normalized it can become after frequent exposure.

Now, that’s not to say San Francisco is unsafe and Mexican cities aren’t. But I’ve spent plenty of time in Mexico City, a huge city with a rough reputation in some places, and the worst violence I’ve experienced was a man winking at me on the street.

Nonetheless, it is important to acknowledge that my experience is not representative of every part of Mexico. The country faces very real security challenges, and many communities experience them far more directly than I ever did.

Mexico is my home, and hearing people automatically associate it with danger is beyond frustrating. Not just because I love the country and its people, but because it isn’t the Mexico I know. My experience isn’t everyone’s, but it has shown me how easily stereotypes can shape the way people see a place they’ve never lived in or even been to. That’s why, whenever someone assumes Mexico is too dangerous to raise a family or attend school, I feel the need to tell them about the home I know instead.

Zella Golden grew up in San Miguel de Allende and is a senior in high school in Marin, California. Golden is completing an internship with MND.

World.title: CDMX declares pan dulce a piece of Intangible Cultural Heritage
World.content:
Mexican pan dulce (sweet bread) has officially been declared Intangible Cultural Heritage of Mexico City, a recognition aimed at safeguarding one of the country’s most fundamental culinary traditions.

The initiative was driven jointly by the city’s Ministry of Culture and the National Chamber of the Baking, Pastry and Related Industries (Canainppa), a trade organization with more than 80 years of history representing Mexico’s bread industry. Beyond advocacy, the chamber provides its members with legal, tax and operational guidance, along with specialized training, as part of its broader mission to strengthen artisanal baking and support the growth of bakery businesses nationwide.

The declaration was approved during the First Extraordinary Session 2026 of Mexico City’s Interinstitutional Commission on Cultural, Natural and Biocultural Heritage. The next step is formal publication in the city’s Official Gazette, expected in September.

According to Julián Castañón Fernández, president of the Canainppa, the declaration is “not merely a technical document. It is a living testament to our traditions, to the creativity of our master bakers and to the cultural scene of Mexico City and Mexico as seen by the world,” he said during the Aug. 7 Session.

Canainppa also submitted a request to the city’s Heritage Commission for pan dulce to be recognized as Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity by UNESCO. That proposal was approved and now moves forward, with backers arguing the tradition goes far beyond food — it’s woven into collective memory, celebrations and everyday customs across Mexican communities.

From conchas to orejas, sweet bread has long been a fixture of Mexican mornings and family gatherings — recently motivating an internet campaign defending its greatness in response to foreign haters.

With reports from Aristegui Noticias and El Financiero

World.title: First Abu Dhabi Bank Misr Posts Strong Profit Growth in Egypt
World.content:
By subscribing you agree to our privacy policy . We never share your email.

Egypt · FINANCE

Key Facts —H1 2024 profit: FABMisr reported net profit of EGP 15.8 billion (about US$330 million) in the first half of 2024, up 139 percent from EGP 6.6 billion in H1 2023. —H1 2025 profit: The bank posted net profit of EGP 8.6 billion (about US$175 million) in the first half of 2025, with total assets of EGP 461 billion (about US$9.3 billion). —Q1 2026 profit: FABMisr earned EGP 6.5 billion (about US$130 million) in the quarter ending 31 March 2026, with net interest income of EGP 7.3 billion (about US$145 million). —Full-year 2024: Net profit reached EGP 26.3 billion (about US$525 million) for the full year, up 153 percent, per FABMisr’s results. —Market position: FABMisr holds roughly 2 percent of Egypt’s banking market by deposits, loans and assets after the Bank Audi Egypt merger completed on 13 June 2022. —Parent backing: First Abu Dhabi Bank is the largest bank in the United Arab Emirates by assets, with a balance sheet of about AED 1.4 trillion (US$380 billion).

First Abu Dhabi Bank Misr, the Egyptian arm of the United Arab Emirates’ largest lender, has delivered sharply rising profits that underscore Abu Dhabi’s deepening financial push into North Africa. The bank’s FABMisr profit growth reflects both strong local operations and a strategic Gulf capital play in Egypt.

Illustrative photo: a Cairo cityscape in Egypt, where FABMisr reported EGP 15.8 billion (about US$330 million) net profit in H1 2024, up 139 percent. (Photo: Mstyslav Chernov, CC BY-SA 3.0, Wikimedia Commons.)

FABMisr profit growth accelerates across reporting periods

First Abu Dhabi Bank Misr reported net profit of EGP 15.8 billion (about US$330 million) in the first half of 2024, a 139 percent increase from EGP 6.6 billion in the same period a year earlier. Net interest income reached EGP 14.6 billion, up 116 percent from H1 2023.

The 2024 surge was flattered by foreign-exchange gains after the Egyptian pound’s sharp devaluation, and reported profits then normalised. In the first half of 2025, FABMisr posted net profit of EGP 8.6 billion (about US$175 million) with total assets of EGP 461 billion (about US$9.3 billion), while the quarter ending 31 March 2026 brought EGP 6.5 billion (about US$130 million) in net profit.

For full-year 2024, the bank recorded net profit of EGP 26.3 billion (about US$525 million), up 153 percent year on year, according to FABMisr’s results. For fiscal year 2025 it reported net profit of EGP 16.7 billion (about US$335 million), which it said marked 5 percent growth after neutralising foreign-exchange effects.

From Bank Audi Egypt to a UAE gateway bank

FABMisr emerged from a cross-border acquisition that reshaped Egypt’s banking landscape. On 13 June 2022, First Abu Dhabi Bank completed the legal merger of Bank Audi Egypt into its operations, rebranding all Egyptian assets under the FABMisr identity.

The merger created a combined Egyptian bank with pro-forma assets of about US$8.1 billion, ranking it among the country’s larger foreign lenders. Analysts describe the deal as a pivotal moment in Middle Eastern banking, sharply expanding FAB’s Egyptian footprint, though its overall market share still sits at around 2 percent.

FABMisr’s network now spans Cairo, Alexandria and strategic Red Sea corridors. That footprint positions the bank to service trade and infrastructure projects linked to UAE capital flows into Egypt.

Egypt as a priority market for Abu Dhabi capital

First Abu Dhabi Bank has signalled appetite for cross-border acquisitions, with analysts naming Egypt, Morocco and sub-Saharan Africa as target markets. Egypt stands out as a priority market due to its large population, under-penetrated banking sector and scope for consolidation among local institutions.

UAE-linked entities have committed tens of billions of dollars to Egyptian projects. These include a highly publicised US$35 billion commitment to the Ras El-Hekma coastal development and a 49 percent Abu Dhabi (ADNOC) stake in a BP-led Egyptian gas venture, into which BP plans to invest about US$1.5 billion.

Recent commentary frames this as an emerging UAE-Egypt-Libya economic nexus. Egypt sits at the centre thanks to its control of the Suez Canal, its Mediterranean coastline and its role as a gateway to African markets.

Gulf banks compete for African financial space

FAB’s Egyptian expansion is one piece of a broader competition among Gulf financial institutions to capture African growth. Banks from Saudi Arabia, Qatar and Egypt itself are also seeking acquisitions or greenfield expansion across the continent.

Gulf banks have built large capital buffers over the past decade, partly due to high oil revenues and domestic prudential regulation. They are now deploying those buffers outward, buying or merging with local banks in high-growth markets with improving regulatory frameworks.

FABMisr’s rising profits strengthen the UAE’s position relative to Saudi Arabia and Qatar in controlling strategic banking channels tied to trade corridors and infrastructure projects. The pattern fits the wider contest for influence covered in Africa: The New Scramble.

Egypt’s megaproject economy needs Gulf finance

FABMisr’s profitability sits against the backdrop of Egypt’s domestic political-economic transformation. Under President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi, Egypt has pursued large-scale projects from new cities to extensive agricultural developments.

One example is the planned Jirian city near Sheikh Zayed, launched in June 2025; Egyptian cabinet-linked reports put its combined cost and expected returns at around EGP 1.5 trillion (roughly US$30 billion), though the government has not disclosed an official cost. Ambitions to cultivate 4.5 million feddans of new agricultural land by 2027 underscore the scale of capital that will need financing and banking services.

Gulf-backed banks like FABMisr can play a crucial role in structuring finance for megaprojects and channelling foreign currency into Egypt. High profits and strong capital positions give the bank leverage in negotiations around project finance, syndicated loans and capital-market deals.

What to watch next for FABMisr and Egypt

Egypt’s repeated currency devaluations and complex foreign-exchange landscape mean headline profit numbers in Egyptian pounds can be volatile in dollar terms. FABMisr and its parent explicitly highlight profit metrics after neutralising foreign-exchange impact.

The bank’s stated interest in Morocco and sub-Saharan Africa signals a long-term strategy to make Abu Dhabi a significant player in African financial systems. The timing coincides with efforts across Africa to increase financial inclusion and develop more robust capital markets.

For investors and professionals watching North Africa, FABMisr’s trajectory offers a clear read on where Gulf capital is heading. FABMisr profit growth in Egypt is now a structural feature of the UAE’s regional power play, not a cyclical blip.

FABMisr reported net profit of EGP 15.8 billion (about US$330 million) in the first half of 2024, up 139 percent from EGP 6.6 billion in H1 2023. Who owns First Abu Dhabi Bank Misr? FABMisr is the Egyptian arm of First Abu Dhabi Bank, the largest bank in the United Arab Emirates by assets with a balance sheet of about AED 1.4 trillion (US$380 billion). How did FABMisr enter the Egyptian market? First Abu Dhabi Bank completed the legal merger of Bank Audi Egypt into its operations on 13 June 2022, rebranding the Egyptian assets as FABMisr and building a network of around 74 branches.

World.title: Kenya Charcoal Prices Hit 78-Month High, Squeezing Urban Households
World.content:
By subscribing you agree to our privacy policy . We never share your email.

Kenya · ENERGY

Key Facts —Retail price: The Kenya National Bureau of Statistics reported an average retail charcoal price of Sh96.79 (about US$0.75) per kilogramme in June 2026. —Price movement: The June 2026 average of Sh96.79 per kilogramme was up from about Sh83.80 per kilogramme in June 2024, based on official KNBS price data. —Historical peak: Business Daily described the June 2026 price as a 78-month high for Kenyan charcoal, the highest since January 2020. —Household burden: In Mombasa, energy accounted for 14 to 35 percent of household budgets, with charcoal representing 10 to 25 percent of energy spending, according to research on Kenya’s charcoal sector. —Regional dependence: Charcoal is used by as much as 80 percent of the urban population in East Africa as a primary cooking energy source, according to a policy brief. —Policy effect: Research found consumer prices more than doubled in some areas after Kenya’s charcoal ban, rising from 7.8 US dollars per bag before the ban to 16.5 US dollars per bag after.

Kenya charcoal prices reached Sh96.79 (about US$0.75) per kilogramme in June 2026, a 78-month high that is forcing low-income urban households to spend more of their budgets on a basic cooking fuel they cannot easily replace.

Illustrative photo: Jua Kali artisans handcraft metal charcoal stoves (jikos) in Kenya, where charcoal reached Sh96.79 (about US$0.75) per kilogramme in June 2026, a 78-month high. (Photo: Monie photography, CC BY-SA 4.0, Wikimedia Commons.)

What the official data shows about Kenya charcoal prices

The Kenya National Bureau of Statistics reported the average retail price of charcoal at Sh96.79 (about US$0.75) per kilogramme in June 2026. Business Daily described the figure as a 78-month high for the commodity, the highest since January 2020, when it stood at Sh152.25 per kilogramme.

Business Daily reported the June 2026 average was up from about Sh83.80 per kilogramme in June 2024, based on KNBS price data, and linked the sustained rise to the government’s 2018 logging ban, persistent household demand and the rising cost of alternative fuels such as liquefied petroleum gas and kerosene. That jump is far above the pace of general inflation and lands directly on households that cook with charcoal daily.

The price rise is not an isolated event. Earlier market snapshots during a logging-ban period showed a four-kilogramme tin selling at Sh84.5 in February, up from Sh79.7 a year earlier, while some areas reported a bag at Sh2,500 and a four-kilogramme tin around Sh120.

Why households feel the squeeze first

Low-income consumers buy charcoal in small quantities several times a week, which makes them more exposed to stockouts and retail mark-ups than households that can afford bulk purchases. When supply tightens, the poorest buyers are the first to pay more.

Research on Kenya’s charcoal sector found that in Mombasa, energy accounted for 14 to 35 percent of household budgets, with charcoal alone representing 10 to 25 percent of energy spending. A price spike of this scale therefore cuts directly into money available for food, rent and school fees.

The alternatives are not always realistic. Studies conclude that punitive charcoal policies can worsen livelihoods for both producers and consumers, with the poorest households least able to shift to liquefied petroleum gas or paraffin when those fuels also become more expensive.

The money and power behind the charcoal trade

Charcoal is not simply a cooking fuel. It is a rent-generating commodity controlled by dealers, transporters and wholesalers who often have better access to capital, information and political connections than the small producers who cut and burn the wood.

Scholarship on African charcoal markets describes them as embedded in resource complexes and “energopolitics,” where access to trees, land, transport and legitimacy determines who captures profits. In Kenya, policy interventions that restrict production can unintentionally strengthen middlemen and grey-market supply chains, because the physical product remains in demand even when formal supply is constrained.

Research on Kenya’s charcoal ban found consumer prices more than doubled in some areas after the restriction took effect. Average consumer prices rose from 7.8 US dollars per bag before the ban to 16.5 US dollars per bag after, while small retail packs climbed from 0.5 US dollars to 1 US dollar per kilogramme.

A regional energy story with geopolitical edges

The Kenyan case sits inside a larger East African energy picture. One policy brief says charcoal is used by as much as 80 percent of the urban population in East Africa as a primary cooking energy source, making price movements a matter of broad political sensitivity.

Regional trade is often cross-border and informal, with bans in one country shifting supply to neighbours and weakening enforcement. In the Horn of Africa, charcoal has been tied to conflict financing and Gulf demand, with United Nations and sanctions-era reporting on Somalia documenting charcoal trade revenues supporting al-Shabaab while Gulf states continued importing Somali charcoal despite bans.

Academic work argues Gulf Cooperation Council states’ demand for Somali charcoal and their broader competition for influence in the Horn have fed patronage networks and intensified regional instability. Charcoal is not a strategic mineral, but it illustrates the same logic of resource dependence, rents and political leverage that shapes the wider competition covered by Africa: The New Scramble.

What to watch next

The immediate losers from the June 2026 price level are low-income families in Nairobi, Mombasa and other urban centres who cannot easily switch fuels. The winners tend to be well-connected intermediaries who can arbitrage scarcity and move product through informal channels.

The next data release from the Kenya National Bureau of Statistics will show whether the Sh96.79 per kilogramme level was a peak or the start of a longer climb. Any new enforcement action on charcoal production or transport would likely push prices higher still, given the pattern documented in earlier ban periods.

For investors and policy watchers, the signal is clear: charcoal pricing in Kenya is a barometer of household stress, regulatory pressure and informal market power all at once. It deserves attention well beyond the kitchen.

Frequently Asked Questions

How much did charcoal cost in Kenya in June 2026? The Kenya National Bureau of Statistics reported an average retail price of Sh96.79 (about US$0.75) per kilogramme in June 2026, which Business Daily described as a 78-month high. Why are Kenya charcoal prices rising so sharply? Supply restrictions, enforcement actions and informal market control by dealers and transporters all contribute to price spikes, with research showing bans can more than double consumer prices in affected areas. Who is most affected by high charcoal prices in Kenya? Low-income urban households are hit hardest because they buy charcoal in small quantities several times a week and have limited ability to switch to alternatives such as liquefied petroleum gas or paraffin.

World.title: Nigeria’s Broadband Speed Jumps 155% as Fibre Connections Triple
World.content:
By subscribing you agree to our privacy policy . We never share your email.

Nigeria · TECHNOLOGY

Key Facts —Median download speed: Nigeria’s fixed broadband median download speed rose from 13.50 Mbps in 2023 to 34.47 Mbps in the first half of 2026, a 155% increase. —Fibre connections: Fibre-to-the-premises subscribers roughly tripled between end-2024 and June 2026, according to Ookla data reported by Nairametrics. —Broadband penetration: Nigeria’s broadband penetration passed 50% in 2025, reaching about 50.58% by November 2025, up from 45.61% at the start of that year. —Subsea capacity: Nigeria is a landing point for eight major submarine cables carrying over 95% of the country’s international Internet traffic, with combined theoretical capacity exceeding 350 Tbps. —Internet traffic milestone: Nigeria achieved 1 Tbps of Internet traffic in the first quarter of 2025, a level the Internet Exchange Point of Nigeria described as a game changer. —Economic projection: The 2Africa cable is expected to add about $9 billion to Nigeria’s gross domestic product by 2025, according to the Nigerian Communications Commission.

Nigeria broadband speed has jumped 155% since 2023, with median fixed download speeds reaching 34.47 Mbps in the first half of 2026 as fibre-to-the-premises connections roughly tripled between end-2024 and mid-2026.

Illustrative photo: reels of optical fibre cable for network deployment. Nigeria’s median fixed broadband download speed rose 155% to 34.47 Mbps by H1 2026 as fibre-to-the-premises connections roughly tripled, per Ookla. (Photo: Asurnipal, CC BY-SA 4.0, Wikimedia Commons.)

What the Nigeria broadband speed data shows

Ookla data reported by Nairametrics on 17 August 2026 shows Nigeria recorded the most consistent improvement in fixed broadband performance among major West African markets over the past three years. Median fixed broadband download speed, excluding satellite connections, climbed from 13.50 Mbps in 2023 to 34.47 Mbps in the first half of 2026.

Median upload speed also improved, rising from about 11 Mbps in 2023 to 25.17 Mbps in the first half of 2026. The gains were not confined to the fastest connections: the 10th percentile download speed nearly tripled from 2.24 Mbps to 6.04 Mbps over the same period.

At the higher end, the 90th percentile download speed rose from 74.37 Mbps in 2023 to 90.04 Mbps in the first half of 2026. This suggests slower connections improved markedly while premium connections saw more modest but still notable gains.

Fibre adoption triples as the bottleneck eases

The speed surge coincides with a threefold increase in fibre-to-the-premises subscribers between end-2024 and June 2026, according to Ookla. A separate report linked to the Nigerian Communications Commission shows fibre-to-the-home subscriptions rising from 84,141 in the fourth quarter of 2025 to 210,065 in early 2026.

That single-quarter jump of roughly 150% is consistent with the broader tripling over the longer period. Mobile broadband has also strengthened, with average 4G download speeds reaching 33 Mbps by end-2025, supported by 2,800 new sites deployed that year.

Broadband penetration passed 50% in 2025, reaching about 50.58% by November 2025, up from 45.61% at the start of the year. Data consumption hit around 1.24 million terabytes in November 2025 alone, reflecting heavy use of streaming, social media, cloud services and enterprise connectivity.

Cheap under the sea, expensive on land

Nigeria has become one of Africa’s key submarine cable landing hubs, sitting at the centre of West Africa’s international connectivity. By 2025, the country was a landing point for eight major submarine cables carrying over 95% of its international Internet and communications traffic.

These systems include SAT-3/WASC, MainOne, Glo-1 and Glo-2, Africa Coast to Europe, West Africa Cable System, Google’s Equiano and the Meta-led 2Africa cable. A detailed engineering study estimates Nigeria is directly connected to at least seven high-capacity international cables whose combined theoretical capacity exceeds 350 Tbps.

Yet domestic fibre distribution remains the constraint. TechCabal describes a paradox: international bandwidth is plentiful and relatively cheap, but spreading that capacity inland from coastal landing points to homes and businesses is expensive, complex and unpredictable.

The West Africa Cable System, a roughly 14,500 to 15,000 km subsea cable, cost about $650 million, or $40,000 to $45,000 per kilometre. By contrast, the federal government estimates expanding Nigeria’s terrestrial fibre backbone to about 90,000 km could require $1.5 billion to $2 billion, with on-land costs often higher due to right-of-way fees, state-level charges, security risks and permitting delays.

US tech giants and the power map

Hyperscale technology companies, notably Google and Meta, are now prime financiers and owners of many new African subsea systems. Google’s Equiano and Meta-led 2Africa both land in Nigeria, anchoring global platforms closer to Nigerian users and entrenching these firms’ ecosystems in the country’s digital economy.

Telecom Review Africa notes that 77 active or planned subsea cable systems serve Africa as of 2025, yet more than half of international bandwidth is concentrated in just five countries: Nigeria, South Africa, Egypt, Algeria and Kenya. This concentration amplifies Nigeria’s strategic importance but also its dependency on foreign corporate infrastructure.

The ownership structure raises sovereignty concerns. Telecom Review Africa highlights that infrastructure carrying African data is increasingly owned by a small number of US technology companies, whose governance structures reflect commercial priorities rather than African national interests.

This places Nigeria inside a wider competition over data routes, standards and surveillance capabilities, a theme explored in Africa: The New Scramble. The West Africa cable outage of 13 March 2024, which disrupted Internet connectivity in at least 13 countries, showed how dependent the region is on a narrow set of routes and landing points.

Regulatory politics and regional ambition

The Nigerian Communications Commission uses infrastructure metrics and outage events to build support for regulatory and fiscal changes. Its leadership has publicly stressed the need for fibre expansion to relieve pressure on mobile networks and avoid congestion as data demand rises.

The commission links new capacity to gross domestic product gains and e-commerce growth, strengthening its case for treating telecom infrastructure as a driver of economic policy rather than a narrow sectoral issue. This gives the regulator more leverage over right-of-way fee harmonisation, open-access fibre models and security standards for landing stations.

Nigeria and Equatorial Guinea have signed a cooperation agreement to deploy a new submarine fibre-optic link, aimed at boosting bandwidth, digital connectivity and regional cybersecurity. Nigerian officials frame such projects as part of a broader effort to integrate African markets under frameworks like the African Continental Free Trade Area.

The result is a patchwork map of power and connectivity. Lagos and selected urban corridors enjoy world-class speeds, while many rural and peri-urban areas still rely on slower, congested mobile networks.

What to watch next

Global subsea cable investments rose from about $0.8 billion in 2015 to $9.7 billion in 2025, with hyperscale technology firms now leading many new projects. The 2Africa cable, launched in 2023, is expected to increase data capacity across Africa by up to 200% and potentially add about $9 billion to Nigeria’s gross domestic product by 2025.

Nigeria achieved 1 Tbps of Internet traffic in the first quarter of 2025, a milestone the Internet Exchange Point of Nigeria’s chief executive Muhammed Rudman described as a game changer for broadband usage and data centre growth. Nigeria’s e-commerce market was estimated at around US$9 billion in 2025 and is projected to approach US$16 billion by 2030, buoyed by wider broadband access and faster connections, according to Mordor Intelligence.

The key question is whether Nigeria can translate foreign-owned subsea capacity into broad-based, sovereign digital development. Stable right-of-way rules, security guarantees in conflict-affected regions and long-term financing will determine whether higher speeds become widely affordable rather than a premium urban service.

Frequently Asked Questions

How much has Nigeria broadband speed increased? Nigeria’s median fixed broadband download speed rose 155% from 13.50 Mbps in 2023 to 34.47 Mbps in the first half of 2026, according to Ookla data reported by Nairametrics. What caused the fibre connection growth in Nigeria? Fibre-to-the-premises subscribers roughly tripled between end-2024 and June 2026, driven by massive undersea cable investment, rising domestic fibre rollout and growing involvement of US tech giants like Google and Meta. Which companies own Nigeria’s submarine cables? Nigeria’s submarine cables are owned by a mix of US technology firms, African telecom operators and consortia, including Google’s Equiano, Meta-led 2Africa, MainOne, Glo-1 and the West Africa Cable System.

World.title: Zambia Arrests 11 Opposition Figures on 2026 Election Night
World.content:
By subscribing you agree to our privacy policy . We never share your email.

Zambia · POLITICS

Key Facts —Arrests announced: Zambia’s government said on 16 August 2026 that 11 people were arrested on the night of the 13 August 2026 general elections. —Government accusation: Authorities said those detained were found with high-grade military weapons and had been planning armed insurrection with foreign nationals. —Opposition response: Presidential candidate Brian Mundubile called the raid an assassination attempt and said the government’s claims were total fabrications. —Election disruption: The Electoral Commission of Zambia suspended vote counting on 14 August 2026, citing violence against officials and ballot paper theft, then resumed the same day. —Partial results: Figures published on 17 August 2026 showed President Hakainde Hichilema extending his lead over Mundubile. —Economic stakes: Zambia is Africa’s second-largest copper producer, and its political stability affects debt restructuring talks with Chinese lenders, Western bondholders and the International Monetary Fund.

Zambia opposition arrests on the night of the 13 August 2026 general elections have triggered competing narratives of a foiled insurrection and a state-orchestrated assassination attempt, deepening investor concern about political risk in Africa’s second-largest copper producer.

Illustrative photo: Zambian President Hakainde Hichilema speaks at a podium bearing the national seal. Partial results published on 17 August 2026 showed him extending his lead over challenger Brian Mundubile. (Photo: Icem4k, CC BY-SA 4.0, Wikimedia Commons.)

Zambia opposition arrests: what happened on election night in Lusaka

Zambia’s government announced on Sunday 16 August 2026 that police had arrested 11 people on the night of the national elections, held three days earlier on Thursday 13 August 2026.

The operation took place at or near the residence of Brian Mundubile, the presidential candidate of the National Reconciliation Party for Unity and Prosperity (NRPUP) and the main challenger to President Hakainde Hichilema.

Authorities said shots were fired from the premises at law enforcement agents, resulting in an exchange of fire during the operation.

Patrick Kangwa, Zambia’s top civil servant, told the BBC that those arrested were found with high-grade military weapons, ammunition and other materials for use in armed insurrection, and had been under surveillance for months.

Competing narratives: insurrection plot or assassination attempt

The government said six named individuals were in custody, including Patrick Mwansa, identified by Kangwa as the husband of Tasila Lungu, daughter of former President Edgar Lungu.

Kangwa said the group was linked to military plans involving foreign nationals and illegal military training camps, posing what he called a serious threat to state security.

Mundubile confirmed he was present at the scene but insisted the raid was an attack on his life, not a legitimate security operation.

The NRPUP rejected what it called spurious and entirely false claims of insurgent activity, framing the arrests as part of a pattern of pre-election intimidation and illegal detentions targeting opposition activists, bloggers and allied business figures.

A pre-election climate of detentions and warnings

The election-night raid capped months of escalating pressure on opposition figures, including the alleged detention of three senior political figures just two days before the vote on 11 August 2026.

Catholic charity Caritas Zambia warned on the eve of the election of arrests and detention of political opponents in undisclosed locations by state agents.

Caritas highlighted the case of Ambassador Martha Lungu Mwitumwa, a former diplomat, and Hannah Katontoka, a blogger and journalist, both arrested on 9 August 2026 when police raided a media centre in Longacres, Lusaka.

The European Union Election Observation Mission reported witnessing an individual seized by armed personnel on the morning of 10 August, noting the episode seemed to give credence to concerns about politically motivated arrests.

Copper, debt and the cost of political instability

Zambia is Africa’s second-largest copper producer, and its political trajectory has direct implications for commodity markets, investor confidence and debt restructuring.

Since Hichilema’s election in 2021, his administration has pursued painful fiscal reforms to stabilise an economy burdened by high external debt, including significant obligations to Chinese lenders, Eurobond holders and multilateral institutions.

The BTI Transformation Index 2026 country report notes that approaching elections increases pressure on Hichilema to adopt populist policy positions and creates incentives to deviate from fiscal discipline, complicating Zambia’s reform trajectory.

For investors, the central question is whether policy stability around mining, tax treatment and debt commitments will be maintained, even as political pluralism is constrained.

Zambia as a great-power laboratory for critical minerals

Zambia is a test case for global debt diplomacy, with negotiations involving Chinese state banks and contractors, Western bondholders and multilateral lenders such as the International Monetary Fund and World Bank.

Great powers view Zambia’s stability and adherence to reform as key to demonstrating the viability of coordinated debt restructuring and securing access to critical minerals essential for the green energy transition.

Political instability or authoritarian drift around the 2026 election could strengthen the hand of security-aligned factions within the ruling coalition who might favour more opaque deals with Chinese or other non-Western partners.

This dynamic fits squarely within the broader competition over African resources and influence tracked by Africa: The New Scramble, where domestic power struggles intersect with global strategic agendas.

What to watch as results are finalised

The Electoral Commission of Zambia temporarily suspended vote counting on 14 August 2026, citing violence against election officials and the theft of ballot papers, before resuming the same day.

Partial results published on 17 August 2026 showed Hichilema extending his lead over Mundubile, placing him on course for victory.

The government has denied accusations of repression, insisting that arrests and restrictions are law-and-order measures aimed at preventing violence and instability.

How international actors respond to the election-night arrests through aid, debt relief, conditionalities or diplomatic pressure will signal the prevailing balance between normative democracy promotion and hard-nosed resource politics.

Frequently Asked Questions

How many people were arrested in Zambia on election night? Zambia’s government said 11 people were arrested on the night of the 13 August 2026 general elections, with six named individuals in custody. What does the Zambian government accuse the detained opposition figures of doing? Authorities accuse them of planning armed insurrection, possessing high-grade military weapons, and being linked to military plans involving foreign nationals and illegal training camps. Who is Brian Mundubile and what does he say about the arrests? Brian Mundubile is the presidential candidate of the National Reconciliation Party for Unity and Prosperity and the main challenger to President Hakainde Hichilema; he says the raid was an assassination attempt and the government’s claims are total fabrications.

World.title: Copper Overtakes Iron Ore at BHP, and Most of It Comes From Chile
World.content:
Chile · Mining

Key Facts Profit Underlying attributable profit rose 30% to US$13.2 billion.

Underlying attributable profit rose 30% to US$13.2 billion. Earnings Underlying EBITDA rose 27% to US$32.9 billion, with a 59% margin.

Underlying EBITDA rose 27% to US$32.9 billion, with a 59% margin. Copper Copper contributed 54% of group EBITDA for the first time, passing iron ore.

Copper contributed 54% of group EBITDA for the first time, passing iron ore. Output Group copper output fell 3% to 1.953 million tonnes in FY2026.

Group copper output fell 3% to 1.953 million tonnes in FY2026. Mine Escondida in Chile’s Antofagasta region produced 1.261 million tonnes of copper.

Escondida in Chile’s Antofagasta region produced 1.261 million tonnes of copper. Payments BHP’s global payments to governments totaled US$12.4 billion in FY2026.

BHP’s FY2026 results show copper became its top earner for the first time, with Chile’s Escondida leading the way. Here’s what it means for the company, the Chilean economy, and investors.

BHP reported its FY2026 annual results on 18 August 2026, and copper overtook iron ore as the company’s biggest earner for the first time. Most of that copper comes from Chile, where BHP operates the world’s largest copper mine, Escondida, in the country’s Antofagasta region.

Escondida in the Antofagasta region is the largest copper mine in the world. (Photo: Internet Reproduction)

Copper becomes the main earner

Copper overtook iron ore as BHP’s biggest profit source for the first time in FY2026. The copper business posted underlying EBITDA of US$18.2 billion, with a 70% margin, making it the clear leader in the company’s portfolio.

This shift shows how global demand for copper, used in electric wiring, renewable energy systems, and electric vehicles, is reshaping the mining giant. Iron ore, long the traditional profit engine, now takes second place.

BHP’s total revenue rose 15% to US$58.8 billion in FY2026. Underlying EBITDA, a measure of operating profit before interest, tax, depreciation, and amortization, climbed 27% to US$32.9 billion, a result executives said was self-funded and record-breaking.

The company’s return on capital employed stood at 26%, a sign of efficient use of its assets. Net debt fell to US$8.7 billion, reflecting strong cash generation and a healthy balance sheet for future investments.

Chile’s role in the copper surge

Chile is central to BHP’s copper story. The company operates Escondida, the world’s largest copper mine, in the Atacama Desert of Chile’s Antofagasta region—a remote, high-altitude area that has become the heart of global copper production.

Escondida produced 1.261 million tonnes of copper in FY2026. That represents a big share of BHP’s total group copper output of 1.953 million tonnes for the year.

BHP also runs the Spence mine in Chile, but the FY2026 production figure for Spence was not available in the results materials. Group copper output fell 3% year on year, partly due to lower volumes at Escondida and Spence.

Despite lower volumes, copper’s high prices and strong margins made it the top earner. The 70% margin on copper EBITDA reflects efficient operations, favorable market conditions, and the high quality of the ore being processed.

What it means for the Chilean treasury

Chile’s government depends heavily on copper revenues, which fund public services, infrastructure, and social programs. When BHP’s copper profits rise, so do the tax payments that flow to the Chilean state.

BHP’s global payments to governments totaled US$12.4 billion in FY2026, according to its Economic Contribution Report, also published on 18 August 2026. That figure covers all countries where BHP operates, not just Chile.

The same report shows a total global economic contribution of US$50.8 billion, which includes wages, taxes, and payments to suppliers across all of BHP’s operations. The company’s global employee wages and benefits alone reached US$5.5 billion.

Global context and outlook

The shift to copper comes as the world invests heavily in electrification and clean energy infrastructure. Copper is essential for electric vehicles, solar panels, wind turbines, and power grids, making it a critical metal for the energy transition.

BHP’s FY2026 results reflect this rising global demand, even though the company’s own copper output dipped 3%. Revenue growth was driven primarily by higher prices for copper and other commodities, rather than increased production volumes.

For investors, copper’s rise is a sign to watch Chilean mining assets closely. Chile holds about a third of the world’s copper reserves, and the country’s mining sector is a key global supplier.

BHP’s net debt of US$8.7 billion is modest relative to its EBITDA of US$32.9 billion, giving the company ample capacity for future investments in copper projects, including in Chile. The company has already flagged growth projects such as Spence SCPY, though specific FY2026 output figures for Spence were not disclosed.

Why this matters for Latin America

If you live in or invest in Latin America, copper is a headline story. Chile’s economy, public spending, and even its currency all move with copper prices, so BHP’s results are more than just a corporate update—they are a macro indicator.

When BHP earns more from copper, it pays more taxes in Chile, which can boost public investment in schools, hospitals, and roads. A stronger copper sector also supports jobs and suppliers across the region, from mining equipment makers to logistics firms.

But lower production volumes at Escondida and Spence are a cautionary note. Operational challenges, water restrictions, or ore grade decline could limit future growth, and investors should watch for how BHP addresses these issues.

Investors should track BHP’s FY2027 guidance for copper production, which will indicate how much Chile can contribute to future profits. The company’s capital allocation decisions—whether to invest more in Chile or elsewhere—will also shape the region’s mining landscape for years to come.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is EBITDA? EBITDA stands for earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation, and amortization. It measures operating profitability before accounting for debt costs and asset wear. How much copper did BHP produce in FY2026? BHP’s total copper production fell 3% to 1.953 million tonnes. Escondida produced 1.261 million tonnes. No FY2026 figure was available for the Spence mine. What is Escondida? Escondida is the world’s largest copper mine, located in Chile’s Antofagasta region. BHP operates it and holds a majority stake.

World.title: Chile Names 12 Experts to Redraw How the State Hires and Pays
World.content:
Chile · Politics

Key Facts Commission The ministerial advisory commission on modernising public employment was presented by President Kast and finance minister Quiroz on 17 August 2026.

The ministerial advisory commission on modernising public employment was presented by President Kast and finance minister Quiroz on 17 August 2026. Deadline The panel has 120 days to deliver proposals to the finance ministry.

The panel has 120 days to deliver proposals to the finance ministry. No chair The commission will not have a president or leader, a deliberate design choice.

The commission will not have a president or leader, a deliberate design choice. Members Twelve experts make up the panel, including Ramiro Mendoza Zuniga, a former comptroller general, and Enrique Rajevic Mosler, a public law academic.

Twelve experts make up the panel, including Ramiro Mendoza Zuniga, a former comptroller general, and Enrique Rajevic Mosler, a public law academic. Remit The commission must listen to civil servants and their associations, and gather views from legislators and experts.

The commission must listen to civil servants and their associations, and gather views from legislators and experts. Purpose The goal is to advance the modernisation of public employment in Chile.

President Jose Antonio Kast has appointed a twelve-member panel to redesign how Chile hires and manages state workers, with proposals due in 120 days.

Chile’s President Jose Antonio Kast launched a twelve-person commission on Monday 17 August 2026 to modernise public employment. The ministerial advisory commission on modernising public employment will advise the finance ministry, led by minister Jorge Quiroz.

The twelve have 120 days and no chair. (Photo: Internet Reproduction)

A Twelve-Person Panel Without a Leader

The commission is made up of twelve experts from law, economics, and public administration. Among them are Ramiro Mendoza Zuniga, a former comptroller general, and Enrique Rajevic Mosler, a professor of administrative law.

Other members include Matias Acevedo Ferrer, Heidi Berner Herrera, and Fernando Claro Valdes. The full roster also features Francisca Diaz Del Rio, Maria Jaraquemada Hederra, Macarena Lobos Palacios, Jorge Rodriguez Cabello, Ernesto Silva Mendez, Cristina Torres Delgado, and Maria Francisca Yanez Castillo.

The commission will not have a chair. That means no single figure heads the body, a design choice that could encourage collective decision-making or, as some might worry, slow it down.

The panel advises the finance ministry, not the presidency directly. Its task is to produce concrete proposals for modernising how the state hires, evaluates, and retains workers.

What the Commission Must Do

The commission’s mandate is to advise the finance ministry on proposals to advance the modernisation of public employment. That includes listening to civil servants and their associations, and gathering the views of legislators and independent experts.

It has 120 days from launch, meaning its proposals are due by mid-December 2026. The deadline is tight, which shows the government wants momentum rather than a drawn-out consultation.

The remit specifically mentions hearing from officials and their unions, a move that suggests an effort to avoid confrontation. It also includes legislators, which could help build political buy-in for whatever the panel recommends.

The finance ministry’s role as the commissioning body means the proposals will likely focus on cost-effectiveness and efficiency, themes that resonate with investors watching Chile’s fiscal position.

The Political Context: Reform After Stalling

Public employment is a sensitive topic in Chile because state payroll costs have been a recurring fiscal concern. Successive governments have promised efficiency, but reform has stalled in Congress, partly due to the rigidity of the administrative statute that governs public sector hiring.

President Kast, in office since March 2026, has made state modernisation a priority. This commission is his first major administrative reform initiative, and it comes during debates over public spending and service quality.

The panel’s broad remit to listen to workers and their associations suggests the government wants to avoid the friction that sank previous attempts. By collecting input from legislators and experts, the commission aims to build a consensus before any bill reaches Congress.

For regular Chileans, the outcome could mean faster government services, more transparent hiring, and better management of public funds.

What the Commission Is Not Doing

The commission is not tasked with cutting jobs or setting specific budget targets. Its mandate is broader: to propose ways to modernise employment practices, not to manage headcount reductions.

There is no mention of outsourcing or privatisation in the commission’s stated remit. The panel will focus on how the state recruits, promotes, and evaluates its workforce, rather than on contracting out services.

The proposals are advisory only. The finance ministry and the president will decide whether to implement them or send them to Congress.

No legal changes happen automatically as a result of the commission’s work.

Because the panel has no chair, decisions may take longer to reach, but that also reduces the risk of one individual dominating the agenda. It’s a structure that encourages negotiation, which might be exactly what Chile’s polarised politics needs.

Market Context and What to Watch Next

The US dollar’s strength against the peso is a factor in any public sector reform. A weaker peso raises the cost of imported goods and can pressure inflation, which complicates public wage negotiations.

Investors should watch whether the commission’s proposals reach Congress by mid-December 2026, which would be 120 days from launch. Any reform that improves state efficiency could boost Chile’s long-term fiscal outlook.

The finance ministry’s role as the commission’s advisor suggests the government wants proposals that are budget-neutral or cost-saving. That could appeal to bond investors watching Chile’s debt trajectory.

Why This Matters for People in Latin America

Chile is often seen as a regional leader in institutional reform, and its public employment practices are watched by other governments. A successful modernisation could set a template for neighbours like Peru or Colombia, which face similar challenges with overstaffed and underperforming state bureaucracies.

For expats working in Chile, the reform could change how government jobs are advertised, hired, and retained. That affects both job seekers and businesses that interact with public agencies, especially those who depend on permits, licenses, or procurement.

For investors, state efficiency is tied to the ease of doing business. Faster permits, better tax collection, and clearer procurement rules all depend on a capable public workforce.

The commission’s work is not just about Chile. It is a test of whether a new administration can deliver structural change in a polarised political environment — a lesson for the whole region.

Frequently Asked Questions

Who created the commission on public employment in Chile? President Jose Antonio Kast and finance minister Jorge Quiroz presented the commission on 17 August 2026. It advises the finance ministry. How many people are on the commission and who are they? There are twelve members. They include former comptroller Ramiro Mendoza, academic Enrique Rajevic, and several other experts in law and public administration. What is the commission’s main task? It must propose ways to modernise public employment, including listening to civil servants, their associations, legislators, and experts. It has 120 days to deliver. Will the commission’s proposals automatically become law? No. The proposals are advisory. The finance ministry and the president will decide whether to implement them or send them to Congress.

World.title: Chile-Argentina Border Pass Reopens After Record 35-Day Snow Closure
World.content:
Chile · Trade

Key Facts Closure The pass shut on 14 July 2026 due to heavy snowfall and strong winds. Snow depth exceeded six metres (about 20 feet) in the high Andes.

The pass shut on 14 July 2026 due to heavy snowfall and strong winds. Snow depth exceeded six metres (about 20 feet) in the high Andes. Reopening The border crossing resumed freight traffic on 18 August 2026 after 35 days. Some outlets counted 34 days because they published before the reopening took effect.

The border crossing resumed freight traffic on 18 August 2026 after 35 days. Some outlets counted 34 days because they published before the reopening took effect. Trade link The pass carries more than 70% of land freight between Chile and Argentina. It sits on the road between Santiago and Mendoza.

The pass carries more than 70% of land freight between Chile and Argentina. It sits on the road between Santiago and Mendoza. Truck backlog More than 2,000 trucks were stranded on the Argentine side, with another 1,600 in Neuquen. Some coverage put the total waiting on both sides above 5,000.

More than 2,000 trucks were stranded on the Argentine side, with another 1,600 in Neuquen. Some coverage put the total waiting on both sides above 5,000. Cost estimate The Camara Aduanera, Chile’s customs chamber, and other trade groups estimate losses near US$200 million. Daily cost per truck ranged from US$300 to US$600 depending on the cargo.

The Camara Aduanera, Chile’s customs chamber, and other trade groups estimate losses near US$200 million. Daily cost per truck ranged from US$300 to US$600 depending on the cargo. Gradual start The reopening is for freight trucks only, from 08:00 to 20:00. Buses and private cars are not yet allowed.

The main road between Chile and Argentina is moving freight again after the longest snow shutdown on record, with losses estimated near US$200 million.

The Paso Los Libertadores, the main highway crossing between Chile and Argentina, reopened on Tuesday 18 August 2026 after 35 days closed by snow. It is the longest closure on record, according to Chilean newspaper La Tercera.

More than seven in ten tonnes of Chile-Argentina land freight go through this pass. (Photo: Internet Reproduction)

A mountain pass choked by snow

The Paso Los Libertadores, also called the Sistema Integrado Cristo Redentor, is the main road link between Chile and Argentina. It crosses the Andes at about 3,200 metres (10,500 feet) above sea level, on the route from Santiago to Mendoza.

Heavy snowfall began in mid-July 2026, piling up more than six metres (about 20 feet) of snow in the mountains. Strong winds and bad weather made the road unsafe for any vehicle.

The closure started on 14 July 2026 and lasted until 18 August 2026. That is 35 days, a record, according to La Tercera newspaper.

Some news outlets reported 34 days because they published the reopening announcement before it took effect.

The pass has been closed before, but never for this long. The previous record was far shorter, making this an extraordinary event for the region.

A costly halt for trade

The pass normally handles more than 70% of land freight between the two countries. With the road shut, trucks could not move goods like fruit, wine, and industrial products.

More than 2,000 trucks were stranded on the Argentine side, and another 1,600 were stuck in Neuquen province. Some reports said over 5,000 trucks were waiting on both sides of the border.

The Camara Aduanera, the customs chamber, and other trade groups estimate the closure cost near US$200 million. This includes parking fees, demurrage, fuel, labour, and cold-chain losses.

Daily costs per truck ranged from US$300 to US$600, depending on the cargo, according to the same industry estimates. Perishable goods like fresh fruit were hit hardest.

The economic impact ripples beyond the border. Delays mean higher prices for consumers and lost revenue for exporters on both sides.

Reopening step by step

Authorities reopened the pass gradually, allowing only freight trucks at first. The schedule is split by direction to manage the flow.

From 18 to 20 August, trucks can cross from Argentina into Chile. From 21 to 22 August, trucks can cross from Chile into Argentina.

All crossings happen between 08:00 and 20:00.

Buses and private cars are not yet allowed. The authorities want to avoid new bottlenecks and ensure the road is safe before expanding traffic.

This phased approach lets officials clear the backlog of waiting trucks without overwhelming the mountain road. It also gives crews time to inspect the route for any remaining snow or damage.

Why this matters for regional trade

For anyone living in or investing in Latin America, this pass is a vital link between two of the region’s biggest economies. Its closure forced companies to reroute or delay shipments, raising costs and hurting competitiveness.

Chile and Argentina trade heavily in fresh produce, wine, machinery, and other goods. The pass is the fastest land route for much of that commerce, so even a few days of closure can disrupt supply chains.

The reopening shows a return to normal after an exceptional event. But it is a reminder how fragile high-mountain trade routes can be.

Trucking companies and importers should plan for future snow seasons. This record closure may not be the last, and having contingency plans is essential.

The economic pain from the closure will linger, as businesses and insurers tally up their losses. Recovery will take time, even with the road open again.

What to watch next

Watch whether the pass reopens to buses and cars in the coming days. That decision will likely come after the freight backlog is cleared.

Also watch how long it takes to move the thousands of waiting trucks. The longer the backlog, the higher the costs for cargo owners.

Finally, look for any official statement about total losses. The US$200 million figure is an industry estimate, not a confirmed government number.

Expect updates from Chilean and Argentine authorities about the pass status. Travelers and freight operators should check official channels before heading to the border.

Frequently Asked Questions

Why did the Paso Los Libertadores close for 35 days? Heavy snowfall and strong winds in the high Andes made the road unsafe. Snow depth exceeded six metres (about 20 feet) in some areas. How much did the closure cost? The Camara Aduanera and other trade groups estimate losses near US$200 million. Daily costs per truck ranged from US$300 to US$600, depending on the cargo. When did the pass reopen? It reopened on Tuesday, 18 August 2026, for freight trucks only. Some outlets reported 34 days because they published before the official reopening. Are buses and private cars allowed yet? No. The reopening is gradual and initially for cargo trucks only. Buses and private vehicles must wait for further notice.

World.title: Enel Starts Building US$80 Million Battery at Chile Solar Farm
World.content:
Chile · Energy

Key Facts Project Finis Terrae BESS is a battery energy storage system, a bank of batteries that stores power for later use.

Finis Terrae BESS is a battery energy storage system, a bank of batteries that stores power for later use. Owner Enel Chile and its renewable arm Enel Green Power Chile are building the project next to the existing Finis Terrae solar plant.

Enel Chile and its renewable arm Enel Green Power Chile are building the project next to the existing Finis Terrae solar plant. Location The site is in the Antofagasta region, in Chile’s northern desert.

The site is in the Antofagasta region, in Chile’s northern desert. Size The system will have 100 MW of power at the connection point. No storage capacity in MWh has been published.

The system will have 100 MW of power at the connection point. No storage capacity in MWh has been published. Cost The investment is about US$80 million.

The investment is about US$80 million. Status Construction has started, but no exact start date or commissioning date has been released.

Chile’s solar boom meets its missing piece: a big battery to save daytime power for the evening.

Enel has begun construction of an US$80 million battery system next to its Finis Terrae solar farm in Chile’s Antofagasta region. The project, called Finis Terrae BESS, will store solar power for use later in the day.

The batteries sit beside the Finis Terrae solar plant in the Antofagasta region. (Photo: Internet Reproduction)

What is Finis Terrae BESS?

Finis Terrae BESS is a battery energy storage system, or BESS for short. Think of it as a giant rechargeable battery—a bank of batteries that stores electricity for when you need it most.

The project is attached to the Finis Terrae solar farm in the Antofagasta region, Chile’s northern desert. Enel Chile and its renewable energy unit, Enel Green Power Chile, are building it, adding storage to an already productive solar site.

The system will have 100 MW of power at the connection point. That means it can deliver up to 100 megawatts to the grid at any moment—enough to power roughly 70,000 homes, based on typical consumption.

One key detail is missing: the storage capacity in MWh. That figure would tell us how long the battery can keep delivering power, but the company hasn’t published it yet.

Without it, we can’t say if it will run for one hour or four.

Why does Chile need batteries?

Chile’s northern desert gets some of the strongest sunlight on Earth, especially in the middle of the day. Solar farms there can generate more power than the grid can actually use at that exact moment.

This oversupply is a real issue: the grid simply can’t absorb all that midday solar energy, so some of it goes to waste. Batteries are the fix—they let you save that surplus and dispatch it later, like when the sun sets and demand spikes.

That’s exactly what Finis Terrae BESS will do. It will charge up during sunny hours and discharge in the evening, shifting solar power to when it’s most valuable.

This makes solar more reliable and helps Chile reduce its reliance on fossil fuels for evening peaks. It’s not just about generating clean power—it’s about using it smartly.

Project details and current status

Enel has started construction on Finis Terrae BESS, but the company hasn’t released an exact start date. The investment is about US$80 million, a big but reasonable bet on storage in Chile’s booming solar market.

The project sits next to the existing Finis Terrae solar farm, a large photovoltaic plant that’s been running for years. By colocating the battery, Enel can store the farm’s output without building new transmission lines—a cost-effective approach.

The Antofagasta region is a prime spot for solar, with some of the highest solar radiation levels in the world. It’s also a region where grid congestion is a known challenge, making storage especially useful.

No commissioning date has been announced either. That’s when the battery will actually start operating and feeding power to the grid, so we’ll have to wait for Enel to provide a timeline.

What this means for Latin American investors and residents

If you live in Chile, you’ve probably seen energy prices swing wildly—sometimes electricity is nearly free at midday, then expensive in the evening. Batteries help smooth that, which could stabilize your bills and make renewables more reliable.

For investors, this project is a sign. Chile is aggressively building solar, but the grid’s limits are becoming a bottleneck.

Storage is the natural next step, and companies like Enel are moving first.

This isn’t just a Chilean story. Across Latin America, sunny countries like Mexico, Brazil, and Peru are watching how Chile handles its solar boom.

Success here could set a template for the whole region.

Battery costs have fallen sharply in recent years, making projects like this economically viable. As more come online, expect to see a ripple effect—more solar, less curtailment, and a more resilient grid from Patagonia to the Atacama.

Looking ahead

Enel hasn’t revealed more details about Finis Terrae BESS’s timeline, but construction is underway. The company may share more as the project progresses, including that elusive MWh figure and a commissioning date.

Without the MWh rating, it’s hard to estimate how long the battery will discharge. The 100 MW power rating is clear, but duration matters—a two-hour battery is very different from a four-hour one.

Observers will watch this project closely once it’s online. If it performs well, it could become a model for other solar plants in Chile and beyond, encouraging more investments in storage.

For now, the message is simple: Chile is moving to add storage to its solar boom, and Enel is leading with a concrete, sizable bet.

Frequently Asked Questions

What does BESS stand for? BESS stands for battery energy storage system. It is a bank of batteries that stores electricity for later use. Where is Finis Terrae BESS located? It is located next to the Finis Terrae solar farm in the Antofagasta region of Chile. How much power will the battery provide? It will have 100 MW of power at the connection point. The storage capacity in MWh has not been published. When will the battery start operating? No commissioning date has been announced yet. Construction has started, but the exact start date is not public.
