World.title: Risky jumps from France's Marseille corniche rise in popularity
World.content:
In Marseille, plunges into the Mediterranean from the corniche are attracting more and more young people in search of thrills. Despite a ban on jumps of more than three metres in place since 2006, the practice, amplified by social media, is gaining ground and is prompting the city council to step up prevention and look for ways to regulate it more effectively.

 

"I started this year. We psych ourselves up, we jump and then we try to move on to another spot," says Dédé, a Marseille resident.

Alongside the regulars from Marseille, there are now tourists, some of whom come especially to try the experience.

"I saw videos online, it caught my attention. I also have friends from here who jump and told me to come," explains Romain, a young Swiss man.

Dominik, who has come from Germany, checked out the best spots beforehand: "This is the third place we have tried and lots of people are jumping here too. You feel safer, because if the people who live here do it, it is reassuring."

Sites under close watch

Behind the spectacular side of the phenomenon, the risks are very real. Every year in Marseille, several people are seriously injured when they dive.

The municipal police monitors the most hazardous spots and has increased patrols to dissuade jumpers.

"We pay particular attention to this area because it is very high. It can be extremely dangerous, especially when landing," explains Céline Lefléfian, head of Marseille's municipal police.

Prevention rather than punishment

Faced with the growing popularity of the practice, the city is also banking on awareness-raising. A civic and public order unit allows young offenders to avoid a fine by attending a session devoted to the dangers of cliff diving.

The city is considering going further by creating dedicated areas. Supervised diving platforms could be installed in zones where jumps can be made under safer conditions.

Marseille city hall is also planning to take its message directly onto social media. An awareness campaign run with influencers is due to be launched soon.

World.title: Shakira and Warren Buffett's son announce rebuilding of schools in Chocó
World.content:
Shakira announced on Monday that she will mobilise funding to rebuild the Technological University of Chocó, damaged by the earthquake that struck Colombia on 10 August, as well as around ten non-university educational centres in one of the five departments worst affected by the quake.

 

The Barranquilla-born artist's donation will not be made directly. The philanthropic organisation Global Citizen will contribute 500,000 dollars (€432,250) and the concert promoter Live Nation, which organised her latest tour, 'Las Mujeres Ya No Lloran', and is also her commercial partner, will provide a further 500,000 at her instigation.

In October 2025 Shakira joined the advisory board of the education fund that FIFA runs with Global Citizen, alongside Serena Williams, The Weeknd and FIFA's own president, the embattled Gianni Infantino. This came several months before her participation as a performer at the recent 2026 World Cup was announced. The Barranquilla-born singer says she has allocated 100% of the royalties generated by the tournament's official song, 'Dai Dai', to that fund.

Shakira will work with Colombian-American philanthropist Howard Graham Buffett, son of tycoon Warren Buffett, one of the world's richest men thanks to multi-billion-dollar stakes in companies such as Apple, Coca-Cola and American Express.

The middle son of the billionaire obtained Colombian citizenship in 2021, under the government of Iván Duque, after investing more than 160 million dollars in projects in the Catatumbo region, including the rebuilding of roads, the replacement of illicit crops and demining work.

"Howard is going to help us, through [the Pies Descalzos Foundation], to build ten new schools in Chocó; that's why it was so important to bring him, that's why it was so important to come today," Shakira told reporters during a visit with Buffett to Quibdó, the capital of Chocó. Buffett's son has overseen Pies Descalzos for two decades; a foundation that has already taken part in the construction of several educational institutions in Colombia.

The visit comes a week after the earthquake, whose epicentre was in San José del Palmar but which affected departments such as Valle del Cauca and Risaralda. The quake has so far left 287 dead, 4,147 injured and 194 missing, according to the latest figures from the National Unit for Disaster Risk Management (UNGRD).

World.title: Ukraine's parliament returns with defence and foreign ministry crises unresolved
World.content:
Ukraine's parliament returns to work on Tuesday after its summer break, reconvening with two of the government's most sensitive wartime portfolios still without heads.

 

When the Verkhovna Rada voted in Prime Minister Sergii Koretskyi’s new cabinet on 16 July, it approved every post except two: defence minister and foreign affairs minister.

For a month now, the defence ministry has been without permanent head, amid Russia's intensifying ballistic missile attacks, an unusual situation for a country defending itself from the full-scale invasion for over four years.

Under Ukraine's constitution only the president can submit nominees for the two posts, since both fall within his direct authority as supreme commander-in-chief and head of the country's foreign policy.

Zelenskyy has so far yet to do so for either ministry.

People hold a minute of silence during a rally to protest the dismissal of Mykhailo Fedorov as Ukraine's Defense Minister in Kyiv, Friday, Aug. 14, 2026. AP Photo

Andrii Sybiha, who had already been permanent head of foreign ministry before the cabinet reshuffle, was kept on as acting foreign minister under a similar Cabinet order.

In the meantime, the defence ministry has been run by Yevhenii Khmara, the former acting head of Ukraine's Security Service (SBU), whom Zelenskyy tasked with the job on 16 July.

The ousted defence minister Mykhailo Fedorov suggested Khmara is not starting from scratch: in an interview on 6 August, he said he had personally handed his successor a detailed "war plan" and walked him through it.

"This was the first thing I did, I showed it to him personally," Fedorov said, adding that he had "explained the logic - how that logic of the war plan then deconstructs into procurement, into development," breaking an overall strategy into hundreds of individual projects, from weapons production to financing.

Demonstrators hold a photo of former Mykhailo Fedorov during a rally to denounce Zelenskyy's decision to dismiss Fedorov, Kyiv, Ukraine, July 24, 2026. AP Photo

Street protests continued

Street protests over Fedorov's removal have continued regardless.

On 16 August Dmytro Koziatynskyi, a war veteran and one of the protest organisers said the aim was "to remind the president of the importance of dialogue between the authorities and society, as well as of the fact that the president himself must bear responsibility for the consequences of all questionable personnel decisions."

A petition read out at the latest demonstration and later handed to a representative of the Presidential Office pointed to one concession already won - Zelenskyy’s decision to replace Oleksandr Syrskyi with Mykhailo Drapatyi as commander-in-chief - while pressing him to explain other contested picks, including Rustem Umerov's move to head the Foreign Intelligence Service.

People march during a rally to protest the dismissal of Mykhailo Fedorov as Ukraine's Defense Minister in Kyiv, late Sunday, Aug. 16, 2026. AP Photo

Notably, the petition focused less on the minister and more on preserving the reform agenda Fedorov had championed, including anti-corruption measures in military procurement, a more accountable chain of command and Ukraine's push into drone and data-driven warfare.

Zelenskyy has said he offered Fedorov "a prominent position in the government" centred on the tech sector, but Fedorov rejected every alternative, saying he will only return as defence minister.

World.title: Could the EU ban smoking? Commission to re-write rules for the next generation
World.content:
As part of its Tobacco Control Framework Evaluation, the European Commission reviewed current tobacco laws and found that, while older rules successfully lowered traditional cigarette consumption, they are nowcompletely outdated and failing to stop a massive surge in digital marketing and novel nicotine products.

 

As a result, the Commission proposed a revision of the Tobacco Taxation Directive (TTD) to implement fresh rules and curb tobacco use. It remains under negotiation after the Parliament failed to adopt a formal position in June 2026, leaving the final decision to the Council of the European Union, where unanimous agreement among member states is required.

Roughly one in four Europeans still smoke or use tobacco regularly. And the problem is increasingly urgent among young people, with data showing that over 11 percent of teens aged 13 to 15 now regularly consume tobacco or trendy nicotine alternatives like flavoured disposable vapes.

“The EU continues to experience roughly 700.000 tobacco-related deaths annually. It remains a leading preventable cause of cancer and cardiovascular disease. From a public health perspective, lower taxes effectively subsidise consumption of a product that kills up to half of long-term users when used as intended”, Professor Martin McKee, Strategic Advisor at the European Public Health Association, told Euronews.

Does the EU have a cigarette problem?

300 billion cigarettes are sold annually in the EU; 24 percent of Europeans smoke, with higher rates among men than women. This massive consumer market is sustained internally, as European factories manufacture more than 220 billion cigarettes each year to meet demand.

Who smokes the most? Eurostat shows ranges from just 8 percent in Sweden up to 37 percent in Bulgaria. Regional disparities are particularly visible among males, with nearly half of the men in Bulgaria (49 percent) and Latvia (48 percent) smoking regularly, compared to less than 10 percent in Sweden.

For women, the highest use is in Greece at 32 percent, while Sweden again reports the minimum at 8 percent. Southern and Eastern European nations consistently report the highest tobacco use, with Croatia and Greece keeping overall smoking rates above 35 percent. Western and Northern European countries like the Netherlands and Denmark have driven their use down to 11 percent and 14 percent respectively.

Smoking poses huge pressures on health sectors. Chronic exposure to tobacco and nicotine results in millions of avoidable hospital admissions every year for respiratory failure, stroke, and ischaemic heart disease. Treating these long-term cardiovascular and chronic obstructive pulmonary diseases drains an estimated €25 billion annually directly from public healthcare budgets.

"Even a delay of a few years in major tobacco-control measures translates into millions of additional smokers, preventable diseases and deaths over time”, warned McKee.

The rise of vapes and IQOS

The peak of traditional tobacco consumption is among citizens aged 25 to 54. However, the market is shifting as younger generations pivot away from traditional cigarettes and towards other products.

These include e-cigarettes or vapes (which heat a liquid with nicotine and flavourings into an inhalable aerosol) and heated tobacco products, such as IQOS, which warm processed tobacco without burning it. Nicotine pouches deliver nicotine orally without containing tobacco leaf.

Health authorities consider these products less harmful than conventional cigarettes, but not risk-free. Studies by several health organisations identified potentially harmful substances, including formaldehyde, acetaldehyde and acrolein, while nicotine itself remains highly addictive. Public health experts also warn that nicotine exposure during adolescence can affect brain development and increase the risk of long-term dependence.

According to the World Health Organization, 11.6 percent of teens aged 13 to 15 in the European region use these products. "Marketing and product design are important drivers. Common features include flavours attractive to young consumers, heavy social-media promotion, lifestyle branding, claims that products are modern, cleaner or safer, and discreet designs that are easy to conceal”, said McKee.

The EU wants smokers to quit

The EU wants to create a “Tobacco-Free Generation” by 2040, where less than 5 percent of the population smokes. This is a cornerstone of Europe’s Beating Cancer Plan. But Brussels lacks the authority for a blanket ban on smoking, because health policy remains a sovereign right for states. Instead, the EU can use its fiscal and regulatory powers to dictate how tobacco is sold and promoted around the bloc.

Over the past decade, it implemented several landmark laws. The 2014 Tobacco Products Directive (TPD II) mandated graphic warnings covering 65 percent of packages and capped e-cigarette nicotine concentration at 20 mg/ml. The Tobacco Advertising Directive (2003) banned tobacco advertising, and the 2001/37/EC Directive completely banned misleading product descriptors like "light," "mild," or "low tar", forcing manufacturers to write bold, black-and-white health warnings on all cigarette packs.

The Tobacco Control Framework Evaluation found these measures successful at lowering traditional smoking rates, which fell from 28 percent to 24 percent among adults. However, it warns that these older laws left gaping loopholes that allowed high-tech nicotine alternatives, like novel products, to thrive unregulated.

The new directive

The Commission's proposed revision of the Tobacco Taxation Directive wants to make tobacco and nicotine products significantly more expensive by raising minimum duties across the EU. For example, it targets a dramatic 139 percent increase in minimum excise duties for standard cigarettes, instantly driving up the baseline retail price.

It also establishes mandatory EU-wide minimum excise taxes on vapes, heated tobacco, and nicotine pouches for the first time, and includes raw tobacco leaf in the EU's electronic tracking system to shut down underground black markets and cross-border tax evasion.

The Commission presented the proposal in July 2025. In June 2026, however, the European Parliament rejected its own advisory report on the file after political groups from across the spectrum voted against a heavily amended compromise text. Because tax legislation follows the EU's special legislative procedure, Parliament's opinion is not binding. The proposal therefore remains under discussion in the Council of the European Union, where unanimous approval from all 27 member states is required before it can become law.

"Many people think the European Parliament is deciding the future excise tax rates. We're not. We're giving an opinion that is not legally binding on the Council”, said Patriots for Europe MEP Tomas Kubin, the report’s rapporteur.

Although the Parliament failed to adopt a formal position, the legislative process continues because taxation is decided by the Council under the EU's consultation procedure.

In parallel, countries are implementing national bans within their own borders. Belgium became the first EU nation to outlaw the sale of disposable electronic cigarettes. France followed by passing its own single-usevape ban, alongside strict legislation that outlaws smoking in public parks, beaches, and school areas. The Netherlands has enforced one of Europe's toughest flavour bans by completely prohibiting every vape liquid except for basic tobacco profiles, while simultaneously drafting laws to raise the legal nicotine purchase age from 18 to 21.

What could change if the directive is adopted

If adopted, the revised directive would place huge pressure on tobacco companies by targeting their profits. The industry remains an economic giant in Europe, with total annual sales reaching approximately €130 billion across the bloc. Companies like Philip Morris International and British American Tobacco would face a direct threat to their business models as the EU introduces these new minimum taxes.

Logistically, manufacturers will no longer be able to use novel products as low-tax loopholes to offset declining traditional cigarette revenues. Furthermore, including raw tobacco into the EU's electronic tracking system will force companies to comply with strict supply chain audits, increasing their administrative and operational costs.

If the proposal is ultimately approved by all member states, European consumers would see significant changes in both the pricing and availability of nicotine products.

Public space restrictions are also tightening across several member states through separate national legislation. Belgium, France and the Netherlands have already introduced stricter rules on vaping and smoking in public places. If the revised TTD is eventually adopted, smokers across the EU would also face significantly higher prices for cigarettes and many alternative nicotine products.

World.title: As Europe’s challenges persist, where are its leaders unwinding this summer?
World.content:
Europe has slipped into its annual summer lull.

 

Brussels has emptied out, national parliaments are in recess, and politicians are looking to make the most of the rare opportunity to step away from the demands of public office.

But for Europe’s political class, switching off can be harder than it looks.

Europe’s crises haven’t disappeared. Russia’s continued bombardment of Ukraine, political tensions in the Middle East, economic uncertainty and wildfires that have ravaged several European countries continue to loom over governments, even as politicians seek to unwind.

Leaders find themselves measuring the length and extravagance of their escapes with particular care to avoid public fallout.

Here’s where some of Europe’s most notable leaders are spending their summer breaks.

European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen

The European Commission chief has not revealed where she is spending her summer break, but on 5 August wished her Instagram followers a good and restful holiday, sporting a pair of sunglasses.

A Commission spokesperson told Euronews that the President, “while currently spending some time with her family, remains in constant contact with her team in Brussels” as well as her team of Commissioners.

“While family time is important, she always follows all critical matters closely, remains fully engaged, and intervenes directly whenever needed,” the spokesperson added, explaining that the President already has official engagements scheduled for next week.

Von der Leyen is known to spend time away from official duties at her family home near Hanover, located on a farm where she keeps horses and has also spoken of raising hens and goats.

In August, she posted a video from the farm in which she introduces a hen named Chikeletta, asking her followers to suggest names for her two newly adopted chicks.

In the past, however, the Commission President’s choice of summer holidays have sparked controversy, with her August 2023 summer retreat at Greek Prime Minister Kyriakos Mitsotakis’ Cretan property sparking sharp criticism.

The EU’s top watchdog, the European Ombudsman, later said that the free-of-charge retreat revealed a “structural shortcoming” in EU ethics rules, and that the “incomprehensible” year-long delay in responding to complaints amounted to maladministration.

French President Emmanuel Macron

The French President is spending time at his official residence of Fort de Brégançon on the Côte d'Azur along with his wife, Brigitte Macron.

It’s the last summer for Macron as head of state, and the venue been the site of several high level visits during his presidency (he even hosted Russian President Vladimir Putin there back in 2019).

He has already been spotted and photographed on a jet ski, prompting critics to accuse him of being disconnected from people’s daily struggles.

French President Emmanuel Macron at the World Economic Forum annual meeting in Davos, Switzerland, Markus Schreiber/Copyright 2026 The AP. All rights reserved.

Yet Élysée officials are briefing French media that the President remains active politically despite his distance from Paris.

On Monday, Macron met mayors of the towns affected by the wildfires that have ravaged the Gironde region in recent weeks, while his Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu has cut his holiday short to visit the affected area.

Macron has also been keeping up his telephone diplomacy while on his retreat, holding calls with Egypt’s President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi, the Crown Prince of Saudi Arabia Mohammed bin Salman, as well as Iraqi Prime Minister Ali Al-Zaidi.

Spain’s Pedro Sánchez

Another European leader grappling with a crisis over the summer break is Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez, whose government has been forced to deal with the mass entry of around 80,000 migrants to the Spanish enclave of Ceuta in late July.

Since the outbreak of the crisis and his visit to the enclave on July 31, the Spanish Prime Minister has switched his Madrid office for his official residence of La Mareta on Lanzarote in the Canary Islands, and according to Spanish media has been conducting official duties from there since 1 August.

Sánchez has interrupted his holidays to hold virtual meetings over the situation in Ceuta, including a ministerial meeting held on Monday.

Spanish Guardia Civil officers stand guard as migrants cross from Morocco into the Spanish enclave of Ceuta, Thursday, July 30, 2026 Antonio Sempere/Copyright 2026 The AP. All rights reserved.

The government acknowledges that the situation in Ceuta is yet to return to normality, and estimates that around 8,000 migrants who crossed in late July remain in the enclave, with around 5,000 thought to be eligible to seek asylum or protection.

Sanchez’s critics, notably from the opposition Popular Party, have slammed the image of normality projected by the Prime Minister at a time of crisis.

Italy’s Giorgia Meloni

Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni is choosing to spend her holidays along with her nine-year-old daughter and sister on the Adriatic coast in Italy’s region of Puglia.

According to Italian media, Meloni could also be joined at a farmhouse in the Brindisi area by friends as well as close allies from her hard-right Brothers of Italy party.

The region on Italy’s heel was also Meloni’s choice of venue when she hosted G7 leaders for a summit two years ago. With the exception of Emmanuel Macron, none of the six leaders she hosted back then are still in post, a reminder of the tumultuous nature of world politics.

Meloni herself faces a crunch election next year. If she does remain in post into the second half of 2027, she could break the record of the Italian head of government with the longest continuous tenure in office.

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz, currently facing low approval ratings, is reportedly taking a short break with his wife Charlotte in Germany, with the Chancellery revealing no further details about his plans.

But, a spokesperson told German media that the Chancellor is “always on duty, always available” and using the downtime to prepare for the September return.

The embattled Chancellor – who is a Roman Catholic — has taken a copy of Pope Leo XIV’s encyclical on artificial intelligence, Magnifica humanitas, with him on his break according to reporting by the Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung.

The encyclical warns of the risks of the technology and calls for it to serve humanity and protect human dignity.

The choice offers a rare glimpse into the Chancellor’s activities beyond his official duties, and could provide a taster of the global issues he is eager to deal with when the legislative term restarts.

Merz, a pro-business Conservative, has in the past suggested EU regulation is becoming a straightjacket for AI innovation.

World.title: Hungary opens sluice and sinks barges to protect nuclear plant as Danube levels fall
World.content:
Water is being diverted into the Danube in Hungary and barges are being deliberately sunk in an effort to raise critically low river levels and prevent another shutdown at the country’s Paks Nuclear Power Plant.

 

Since noon on Monday, an additional 20 cubic metres of water per second has been released into the main Danube from the Ráckeve-Soroksár branch at Dömsöd, around 50 kilometres south of Budapest. The measure has raised the river level by about two centimetres.

Further downstream at Paks, about 100 kilometres south of the Hungarian capital, two barges are also being prepared for controlled sinking. Water is being pumped into their hulls so that they settle on the riverbed, forming a temporary sill designed to raise the water level near the nuclear plant.

Officials hope the intervention will prevent another shutdown of the plant's penultimate operating turbine as the Danube continues to fall.

Work is also under way on a permanent sill across the river between the Paks plant and Dunaszentbenedek, a village on the opposite bank. The Hungarian government approved the emergency project last week following a site inspection and a unanimous recommendation from water management, energy and defence experts.

The Tassi sluice at Dömsöd has been opened - 17 August 2026 Euronews/KR

The structure will initially use 35,000 cubic metres of rock, with the amount later increasing to 110,000 cubic metres and the project is progressing at "breakneck speed" according to officials.

Tuesday and Wednesday are expected to be critical, with the Danube forecast to fall by a further 14 to 15 centimetres.

However, conditions could begin to improve from Thursday, when rainfall in the Danube's Austrian catchment area is expected to start pushing river levels higher.

World.title: Fact check: How do I spot propaganda?
World.content:
Across the world, politicians use propaganda to manipulate the thoughts and actions of others. It's a strategy deployed by democracies and dictatorships alike. How, then, can I detect propaganda?

The 2026 US-Iran war was not just fought on the battlefield, but also across social media.

AI-generated animations inspired by "The Lego Movie" showcased Iran's military power, while another animated video depicted a supersized version of US Vice President JD Vance rampaging through Tehran like Godzilla.

Accounts sharing this kind of content have amassed millions of views and offer a powerful example of propaganda in the age of artificial intelligence.

They also illustrate how propaganda, while far from a new phenomenon, continues to evolve alongside technology.

So, what is propaganda? And how can you spot it?

DW Fact check offers tips to help you navigate today's information landscape.

Defining propaganda

Artificial intelligence is dramatically changing the way propaganda is created and distributed Image: X

Propaganda is often described as the deliberate use of information by governments, politicians and other actors to shape people’s beliefs, attitudes or behavior.

It relies on the selective presentation of information, emphasizing certain facts while omitting or misrepresenting others.

Propaganda is not only deployed by authoritarian countries like Russia, China and North Korea; it can be found all over the world.

A key difference between systems is that propaganda in authoritarian states is often heavily centralized and tightly controlled.

In democratic societies, propaganda is often more pluralistic, produced by a wider range of actors.

Moreover, freely accessing alternative media outlets and information is far more straightforward in democracies.

What is the purpose of propaganda?

Talking to DW, Piers Robinson, a political scientist with the Organisation for Propaganda Studies, said propaganda can persuade someone to act or behave in a particular way.

He cited the example of how US politicians worked to convince the public to support the 2003 invasion of Iraq.

"In that case, famously, they exaggerated intelligence about weapons of mass destruction to make Iraq appear a bigger threat than it really was," said Robinson.

No weapons of mass destruction were ever found in the country. Images presented by the CIA purporting to prove their existence constituted misinformation deployed for propaganda purposes.

The Iraq War demonstrates another key aim of propaganda: vilifying political opponents, rival countries, or cultures or values seen as undesirable or threatening.

US President Donald Trumpis a case in point.

US President Donald Trump deleted his own social media post where he portrayed himself as a Jesus-like figure Image: Vuk Valcic/SOPA Images/ZUMA/picture alliance

Researchers who have studied his political rhetoric point to his frequent use of name-calling as a technique for discrediting political opponents and to his use of exaggerated claims to portray undocumented immigrants disparagingly.

Propaganda is not always negative. It's also designed to cast politicians and governments in a positive light, said Pavel Koshkin, a senior research fellow at the Institute for US and Canadian Studies of the Russian Academy of Sciences.

In Russia, Koshkin said, state-sponsored propaganda is utilized to create a "democratic image of Russia."

What role do media outlets play in spreading propaganda?

Media organizations can spread and amplify propaganda messages either knowingly or by mistake, Christian Mihr of Reporters Without Borders (RSF) told DW.

Russian state-funded broadcaster RT, for instance, is often accused of serving as a Kremlin mouthpiece. Its coverage largely reflects the Russian government's official position.

RT is accused by many of peddling a pro-Kremlin narrative Image: Jaap Arriens/NurPhoto/picture alliance

Ideally, media organizations play the opposite role: as watchdogs to sniff out and debunk propaganda.

Indeed, media researchers say this is one of the most important tasks expected of journalists.

RSF's Mihr said journalists are in an ideal position to help contextualize political propaganda by asking lawmakers tough questions and interviewing independent experts.

And what about AI-fueled propaganda?

Artificial intelligence is dramatically changing the way propaganda is created and distributed.

While producing propaganda once required hours or days of work, AI tools can now generate images, videos and audios in minutes.

This allows governments and other actors to adapt messages quickly and tailor them to different audiences, platforms and languages.

The 2026 US-Iran war was not just fought on the battlefield, but also across social media with large amounts of AI-generated animations Image: instagram

That's where the term "slopaganda" comes in. It combines propaganda and slop, a term often used for low-quality, AI-generated material.

Consider the AI-generated images mentioned above that circulated during the 2026 US-Iran war.

Their widespread use has led some observers to describe the conflict as a "slopaganda war", highlighting the emergence of a new form of online information warfare.

So, with all this in mind, how can you tell whether you’re looking at propaganda?

Tips to detect propaganda

If you want to detect propaganda, put every claim under the lens Image: Andy Wong/AP Photo/picture alliance

Although propaganda is often subtle, there are, nevertheless, ways of identifying it.

One of the most effective ways is to look closely at where the information comes from.

Did a government official or agency publish the message? Does it come from a state-funded media outlet? Or from an account linked to one?

Take a moment to learn more about the source.

Who runs the source? Is there a disclosure included somewhere? Can I find information about how it is funded? Is its purpose clear?

The more information you can find out, the better you will be able to evaluate a source. And don’t forget: a lack of transparency is often a red flag.

Once you've analyzed where the information comes from, it's time to look at the content itself.

Be wary of information that provokes strong emotions, both positive and negative. Propaganda and "slopaganda” are often designed to trigger emotional reactions rather than encourage critical thinking.

Take a moment to pause if a post makes you feel angry, fearful or outraged. Or if it appeals strongly to your personal, religious, ethnic or national identity.

In addition, look carefully at what the post actually says. Reading about the topic, consulting independent sources and comparing different perspectives can help you assess a message critically.

Ask yourself the following questions:

Is the post presenting complex issues in simple, black-or-white terms?

Is it claiming that only one viewpoint is acceptable?

Is it demonizing groups or opponents?

Is it using facts selectively and leaving out important context?

Is it using statistics in a misleading way?

Finally, be skeptical of volume. As we saw above, "slopaganda" relies on spreading large amounts of low-quality, emotionally charged content.

One of its aims is to create the impression of consensus: the more often people see a message, the more likely they may be to perceive it as widely accepted.

So if you repeatedly see a message or come across the same claim, take a step back and investigate further.

This article was first published in 2022 and has been revised to incorporate new developments and trends. The experts featured were interviewed for the original article, and their insights continue to provide valuable context for the issues discussed.

This article is part of a DW Fact check series on digital literacy. Other articles include:

And here you can read more about how DW fact-checks fake news.

Edited by Josh Axelrod.

World.title: Do not inhale! How wildfire smoke 'affects the whole body'
World.content:
Wildfires destroy lives and livelihoods. But survivors and firefighters also suffer long-term harm to their health. A growing body of research suggests particulate matter (PM2.5) in wildfire smoke is a major culprit.

Researchers are beginning to understand the long-term impact of wildfire smoke exposure on human health. And it's not good. "Your whole body is affected," said Yang Liu, Professor of Environmental Health at Emory University in Atlanta. "Wildfire smoke causes oxidative stress to your system and exacerbates or accelerates the development of diseases."

In a study published in January 2026 , Yang Liu and other researchers found that repeated exposure to even moderate amounts of smoke increases the risk of stroke among older adults.

A month later, another study found that long-term exposure to wildfire smoke had contributed to an average of 24,100 deaths a year in the United States between 2006 and 2020.

Wildfire smoke contains a mixture of hazardous air pollutants. But one of the most aggressive components appears to be tiny specks of particulate matter, known as PM2.5.

PM2.5 is made up of soot, dust, and other substances that act like sponges, binding toxic metals and organic compounds to them.

If inhaled, PM2.5 particles can get into the lungs and bloodstream, from where they cause inflammation and damage to various other organs in the body.

Long-term exposure to PM2.5 has been linked to lung diseases like asthma, as well as heart disease, diabetes, dementia, and cancer.

Wildfire smoke is particularly dangerous for pregnant women. It can increase the risk of premature births and low birth weight.

What makes PM2.5 in wildfire smoke so toxic

Wildfire PM2.5 is particularly toxic due to complex mixtures of burning materials found at any site, which can differ between rural fires and those that spread to urban areas.

"It really does depend on the location of the fire. It might even vary from block to block — the smoke may consist of different components," said Mary Johnson, a principal research scientist in the Department of Environmental Health at the Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health.

Researchers have detected heavy metals and other potentially carcinogenic compounds, such as PFAS, or "forever chemicals" in wildfire smoke Image: Tomas Cuesta/AFP/Getty Images

Johnson led an international team that studied toxic substances in wildfire smoke in a group of healthy firefighters and civilians who had recently been exposed to wildfire smoke. They wanted to understand how these toxins disrupt immune cell function and increase the body's susceptibility to infections and chronic diseases.

The researchers found mercury and cadmium — both heavy metals found naturally in plants and soils, as well as in man-made materials. They also found carcinogenic compounds and so-called forever chemicals, known as PFAS.

PFAS are synthetic chemicals used in many everyday products and building materials. They have been linked to various cancers and metabolic conditions.

Their findings led them to suggest future research should focus on developing treatments for vulnerable groups like children and elderly people and those with chronic health conditions.

Wildfire smoke becomes more toxic over time and distance

Wildfire smoke becomes more dangerous as it ages, undergoing chemical reactions that increase its ability to damage cells.

Researchers in Greece found that smoke can get up to four times more toxic in the days following a fire. It can also travel long distances quickly and spread to areas thousands of miles away from the original source of the fire.

"If there is no rain to wash out these particles, they can stay in the atmosphere for ten days or sometimes more. They can go around the whole hemisphere and come back to the departure point within this time," said Nikolaos Mihalopoulos, director of the Institute for Environmental Research and Sustainable Development at the National Observatory of Athens.

During the Canadian wildfires of 2023, for example, 6,000 fires burned 15 million hectares of land, causing "long-range PM2.5 pollution" to spread across North America and even reach Europe and Asia.

In a paper published in September 2025, researchers estimated that about 5,400 acute deaths in North America and about 64,300 chronic deaths in North America and Europe could be linked to PM2.5 exposure from the 2023 Canadian wildfires.

However, it is worth noting that other sources of air pollution — traffic exhaust fumes, industrial emissions, and burning fuel for cooking — still cause more health problems overall because people are exposed to them daily.

Wildfires on the rise: Rethinking prevention across Europe To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

"When we look at what really drives mortality in the population as a whole, it's still all these other sources [of air pollution] that are really responsible for so many deaths," said Cathryn Tonne, an environmental epidemiologist at the Barcelona Institute for Global Health.

How to protect yourself against wildfire smoke

Wildfire smoke is uniquely toxic, especially for people living near areas prone to fires.

"The more you can do to minimize exposure, the better," said Johnson, who recommends staying indoors during and immediately after fires, using filters on heating and air conditioning systems, keeping N95-grade masks available, and ensuring vulnerable people have emergency supplies of medication and inhalers readily accessible.

Ahead of fire seasons, people should clear their properties of flammable materials and set up neighborhood monitoring groups that look out for early fire signs and help stop small fires from becoming catastrophic ones.

Edited by: Zulfikar Abbany

World.title: Meta trial over social media harm to children begins
World.content:
Four US states are taking Meta to court, accusing the social media giant of deliberately making Facebook and Instagram addictive for children. They're seeking damages and changes to the company's apps.

A landmark trial seeking to hold Meta accountable for the alleged harm its social media platforms cause children is set to begin in California on Tuesday.

Four US states, California, Colorado, Kentucky and New Jersey, argue the company misled the public about the safety of Instagram and Facebook and deliberately made the apps addictive for minors.

Lawyers for the states also allege Meta is violating privacy laws by routinely collecting data on children under 13 without their parents' consent.

The states are seeking around $200 billion (€173 billion) in damages as well as significant changes to Meta's core platforms.

They are part of a coalition of 29 states that sued the tech giant in 2023 for allegedly building addictive features into its apps.

The trial is taking place at the federal courthouse in Oakland, California Image: Manuel Orbegozo/REUTERS

What to expect during the trial

Opening statements were set to get underway in the federal court in Oakland, a short drive from San Francisco, on Tuesday.

Among the star witnesses expected to testify during the proceedings is Meta founder and chief executive Mark Zuckerberg.

Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg is expected to testify during the trial Image: Ryan Sun/AP Photo/dpa/picture alliance

Former Meta employee and expert witness Arturo Bejar is also expected to testify, despite the company's efforts to block his appearance.

According to court documents, lawyers for the states are to question him for three hours about Meta's safety practices and whether the company publicly misrepresented what it knew.

Eight people are serving on an advisory jury, but the final decision in the case rests with Judge Yvonne Gonzalez Rogers.

What have both sides said about the case?

Kentucky Attorney General Russell Coleman described the case as "the largest consumer protection lawsuit in American history."

"We'll show a jury that Meta concealed what it knew about the harm its products cause young people because looking away was more profitable," he said in a statement.

Meta, meanwhile, said it strongly disagreed with the allegations.

"We are proud of our record in protecting teens on our platforms and the amount of effort that we've put into developing protections over the years, even before these cases were ever filed," the company said.

"We look forward to showing the judge and the jury those facts in court," it added.

The trial is set to last six to eight weeks, with a verdict expected by October.

World.title: Germany updates: new drone research center to be opened
World.content:
08/18/2026 August 18, 2026 Germany opens new drone research center

A new drone research center is set to open in the eastern German state of Saxony-Anhalt on Tuesday, two weeks after an incident involving a drone at an airport in nearby Leipzig.

The new facility at the German Aerospace Center (DLR) in Cochstedt, just south of the city of Magdeburg, will be officially opened by Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt (CSU), Research and Technology Minister Dorothee Bär (CSU) and Saxony-Anhalt state premier Sven Schulze (CDU).

The center will conduct research into new drone security technologies and test them under realistic conditions, combining scientific theory with the practical demands of Germany's security services.

"The arms race in drone technology calls for specific research facilities in order to keep up," Dobrindt said following the recent incident in Leipzig, when an explosive-laden drone was discovered close to several Ukrainian cargo planes. State prosecutors spoke of a "serious attack on Germany's transport and logistics infrastructure" and are continuing their investigations.

An interior ministry spokeswoman said on Monday that "a lot of research, development and observation" is required in order to determine what exactly Germany needs to improve its anti-drone capabilities, and said that the new Cochstedt facility would be a "key component" in this endeavor.

The German government is particularly concerned about developments in AI-controlled drones which can continue towards their targets even when jammers interrupt their connections. Another key aspect involves the accurate identification of different types of drones in order to implement the most effective form of defense.

World.title: India: Testing agency revamp follows renewed criticism
World.content:
08/18/2026 August 18, 2026 Seafarers' union says crew being forced to transit Strait of Hormuz

The Forward Seamen's Union of India (FSUI) has flagged an incident in which a commercial vessel's captain is allegedly being pressured to force its crew to transit through the "high-risk" Strait of Hormuz.

"Managers of Marshall Islands-flagged vessel AM Pioneer are pressuring the Master to force its 16 Indian crew to transit the high-risk Strait of Hormuz," the union said in a post on X. "The crew has clearly refused. They will not put their lives in danger," it added.

The post included a video in which the vessel's captain said that the company had initially directed him to transit through the strait once it was open and it was safe to navigate. "Now from last week the Company is forcing us to cross through Hormuz and go to Fujairah," he said, referring to the port city in the UAE.

"They tried to arrange one security and requested the American defence to give us air support to pass through Hormuz. The company is trying to push us through Hormuz in a crooked way and put our lives in danger," he said.

The crew "will not sail under dark conditions with communications switched off. No seafarer should risk death for owners' profits or convenience," the FSUI said, demanding immediate repatriation with full wages and dues.

The union also called on the Indian government to intervene. India's foreign ministry or shipping ministry has not publicly commented on the matter so far. India has repeatedly condemned attacks on commercial vessels passing through the Strait of Hormuz and said the safety of the seafaring community is a high priority.

Indian nationals make up around 12% of the global merchant shipping workforce, leaving them especially exposed to the risks of the conflict in the Middle East.

World.title: Tupac Shakur murder trial opens as prosecutors say 'Keffe D' ordered 1996 killing
World.content:
A trial is finally underway 30 years after rap artist Tupac Shakur was killed in a drive-by shooting. The case was long regarded as one of the nation's most prominent cold cases.

The murder trial over Tupac Shakur's 1996 killing opened with prosecutors arguing that Duane "Keffe D" Davis planned the shooting.

Almost three decades after the drive-by shooting they opened their case by telling jurors the rapper was shot dead in an act of gang revenge masterminded by a mobster.

“Let’s be clear, Duane Davis did not pull the trigger. But he did plan the shooting in retaliation of the beating of his nephew,” Chief Deputy District Attorney Binu Palal said.

Davis, a one-time leader of the South Side Compton Crips gang, is charged in Clark County, Nevada, with a single count of murder using a deadly weapon.

The 63-year-old has pleaded not guilty.

What the prosecution said about 'shot caller' Davis

Davis ordered the killing after his nephew, Orlando "Baby Lane" Anderson, had been beaten by a rival gang, Chief Deputy District Attorney Binu Palal told a court in Las Vegas Tuesday.

Palal showed videos Tuesday of Shakur's entourage attacking Anderson.

"Then, two and a half hours later... Tupac is gunned down in a drive-by shooting from a white Cadillac in an act of revenge," the prosecutor told jurors.

Palal said that Davis — who has been dubbed by the authorities as a "shot caller" — did not pull the trigger but "he did plan the shooting in retaliation of the beating of his nephew".

Palal went on to tell the jury: "Remarkably, you will learn that from Duane Davis himself," referring to Davis' previous interviews with law enforcement and the media, as well as his autobiography, where the accused describes Shakur's killing.

Davis said in the interviews and his 2019 memoir, "Compton Street Legend," that he was riding in the car from which Shakur was shot.

In an interview with a federal task force probing another killing, Davis spoke of the Shakur shooting. He described handing a gun to the men in the backseat of the white Cadillac that fired on the rapper's black BMW.

On Tuesday, prosecutors played audio of Davis explaining the moment Shakur was shot.

Davis' defense rails against 'sloppy' investigation

Representing Davis, attorney Michael Sanft called the prosecution's narrative "fiction" during the defense's opening statement.

Sanft said prosecutors had no real proof that his client was culpable. He said that after 30 years a police investigation has repeatedly failed to turn up a definitive version of events.

He called the investigation "biased," "sloppy" and "incomplete."

"Just look at ‌the actual facts. What facts do you have to support any of what Keffe D said in any of his interviews or the book?" Sanft told the jury.

The defense had fought to keep Davis' book out of the trial. Image: Steve Marcus/REUTERS

Sanft further said the accounts he gave in interviews and his memoir ccould not be corroborated.

Davis was seen at the trial wearing a blue suit and tie. He was also seen scanning the public gallery during testimony.

As per Nevada law, Davis can be charged with murder if he took part in the crime without firing the gun himself.

If convicted, he faces the possibility of life imprisonment without parole.

Meanwhile, the trial is expected to last up to six weeks.

Tupac Shakur — a cultural icon

Shakur, also known as 2Pac, was 25 when he was wounded in a drive-by shooting on Sept. 7, 1996.

He succumbed to his injuries in hospital six days later.

Shakur, who also went by the stage names 2Pac and Makaveli, is considered one of the most influential rappers of all time Image: Death Row Records/dpa/AFP/picture alliance

Although his death cut his immensely popular music career short, Shakur remains one of the most influential and versatile rappers of all time.

Shakur's music often addressed issues facing Black Americans.

He was also a key figure in a hip-hop rivalry pitting the US East Coast against the West Coast.

Edited by: Louis Oelofse

World.title: Philippines: student livestreams school shooting
World.content:
Two students, including the shooter, have been killed and at least two others wounded at a private university campus in the southern port city of Zamboanga.

A high school student opened fire at a private university campus in the Philippines on Tuesday, killing a fellow student and wounding two others before turning the gun on himself.

The shooting, which the student reportedly livestreamed using a body camera, took place at about 7:50 a.m. local time at Ateneo de Zamboanga University in the southern port city of Zamboanga, about 800 kilometers (500 miles) south of the capital, Manila.

Hundreds of students were evacuated after gunshots were heard in the high school building, which is located on a secure campus separate from the university's main campus.

Regional police said a ninth-grade student, typically ages 14-16, brought a "pistol and rifle inside the school campus" and opened fire in a classroom.

"One of the focuses our investigation will look into is how the suspect brought the firearms into the school," said a spokeswoman.

"The investigation is ongoing ... We are still trying to identify the motive."

A few hours after the shooting, police said the situation was under control. They requested that parents and guardians of students remain calm and follow advice issued by the school to pick up their children.

Police chief Jose Melencio Nartatez also called on the public to "refrain from sharing unconfirmed reports, photos, or videos that may cause unnecessary concern," adding that authorities would "provide verified information as appropriate."

People gathered outside the Ateneo de Zamboanga University campus following the shooting. Classes at the university were suspended. Image: Nonoy Lacson/REUTERS

Philippines: How did the shooting unfold?

In a video that was seemingly livestreamed on Facebook and circulated by local media, the barrel of a gun is seen moving down a hallway in the style of a first-person shooter video game before being aimed into a classroom and fired, according to the AFP news agency.

"In the video, we see that he first shot at the teacher who was sitting at a desk," Zamboanga city mayor Khymer Olaso told a local radio station. "It seems he missed, then moved to another room [and] shot another student there."

Other children in school uniforms can reportedly be seen screaming and rushing for an exit.

The alleged shooter's Facebook account has since been disabled, and classes at the university were suspended.

Are school shootings common in the Philippines?

School shootings are rare in the Philippines where gun ownership is tightly regulated.

However, a large black market for firearms exists, and three students were killed while 20 others were injured in a shooting in the eastern city of Tacloban in June.

Last month, the Ateneo de Zamboanga campus became one of many educational institutions across the country to conduct active-shooter drills.

"We are all aware that security measures have been stepped up in schools," said the police spokeswoman.

World.title: Zambia's Hichilema wins second presidential term
World.content:
Hakainde Hichilema won over 60% of the vote in the first round of Zambia's presidential election, which also saw authorities launch raids against leading opposition figures on election night.

Zambian President Hakainde Hichilemahas secured another 5-year term, the country's election commission announced early on Tuesday.

Hichilema — who was widely expected to win — secured 61.4% of the 5 million votes cast in the presidential race held last Thursday, while his main election rival Brian Mundubile received 38% votes, according to the tally released by the Electoral Commission of Zambia.

"I therefore declare, Hichilema Hakainde S, to be president-elect of the Republic of Zambia this 18th day of August, 2026," commission chairperson Mwangala Zaloumis said in a statement.

Out of the total 226 constituencies in the southern African nation, five had not been tallied but Zaloumis said those results were "not likely to materially influence the overall result of that election."

Raids against 'militia activity' on election night

The election saw the opposition claiming intimidation, arrests, violence and irregularities.

Mundubile had alleged irregularities in the counting but Hichilema backers said he was lying.

While the vote was largely peaceful, the night of the election saw authorities arresting 11 people, including leading opposition figures, in what the government called a raid against "militia activity".

Mundubile's NRPUP party slammed the government's claims that its members were involved in militia or insurgent activity.

The NRPUP said shots were fired during the raid at Mundubile's home.

Mundubile's, a former provincial minister, decried the police raid an attack on his life.

Can Zambia trust election referee? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Vote counting paused after reports of ballot theft

The vote counting was also suspended last Friday after the commission reported attacks against polling officials and theft of some ballots.

The counting restarted hours later under tightened security.

International observer missions, including the European Union, said that the nearly six-hour pause was a threat to the credibility of the electoral process, along with voter confidence.

Voters focus on Hichilema's economic record

The ballot marked a seventh run for presidency for 64-year-old Hichilema, who has been in power since 2021.

Hichilema took charge of a copper-rich nation in the midst of a pandemic-era debt crisis and a strong economic downturn. His first term saw Zambia restructure its debt and lower inflation, which Hichilema used for his more recent economic campaign.

"We are truly humbled by the trust you have placed in our hands," he said after emerging victorious on Tuesday.

"To those citizens who preferred the ideas presented by our opponents, we hear you, and we will continue to work for you."

His main challenger, Mundubile, had put his hat in the ring for the first time but his hopes to become the head of state were dashed.

He had rallied against Hichilema, telling Zambians that the country's improving macroeconomic indicators had ‌ made little difference to their actual living standards.
