From this perspective, the approach is entirely sound. However, we must ensure this does not lead to endless postponements. The state must actively work on this by defining clear criteria in legislation to specify what constitutes fluency in the Abkhaz language.

This requirement should apply not only to the parliament but also to the executive branch. Implementing it within the judiciary will be more complex, as it requires extensive work to adapt the full body of legal terminology, which demands highly specialized legal expertise.

Inal Khashig: There are terminologies. All of that exists.

Astamur Tania: I know that preliminary work has been carried out—mostly at the level of compiling dictionaries of legal terms, as far as I am aware. However, implementation within the judiciary is far more difficult purely due to professional constraints.

That is why I believe the presidential initiative reflects today’s realities. It creates a space for compromise among political participants and allows us to develop proper criteria for assessing Abkhaz language proficiency.

If we fail to reach an agreement and leave everything as it is—which could easily happen if the president’s proposed law fails to pass—we will remain at a standstill. The entire process could degenerate into a formalistic routine, similar to what we witnessed during the presidential elections, and only spread further.

Therefore, as an initial step, I view this approach as very reasonable. Since there is no discrimination involved, I see no basis to claim it is unconstitutional.

Inal Khashig: I have my own perspective on this, though doubts constantly trouble me. The initiative grants a deferment to non-ethnic Abkhazians, but I am convinced that in five years, by 2032, we will find ourselves with the exact same results.

Astamur Tania: That certainly cannot be ruled out.

Inal Khashig: Indeed. But my concern is the formalistic approach toward the Abkhaz language itself. For instance, the language law was adopted in 2007 and was meant to take full effect in 2015, requiring the entire Abkhaz bureaucracy to be fluent in the state language.

Yet, even if a good half of them are fluent today, we should consider ourselves lucky—especially since no actual testing or measurements were ever conducted.

Astamur Tania: If at least a “bad half” had command of it.

Inal Khashig: Yes, yes. I am afraid that, strictly speaking, we will simply do this—formalize the commission itself, which we will bring to formal absurdity. Like, here is a good guy, he knows 10 words.

Astamur Tania: If we do not change our attitude toward our state, then in the Abkhaz language, and in security, and in the economy, we will have roughly the same result. You are right. This is a broader question than the Abkhaz language. It is just that now it is at the peak of relevance due to the debates in parliament and in society. In fact, this is a question of our attitude.

Various arguments are brought up that the quality of parliamentarism may drop from this. It seems to me that despite the absence of this norm, the quality of our parliamentarism was declining anyway. So the problem, after all, is not only in the Abkhaz language. This is a hackneyed phrase that we always get the government we deserve, that it is a reflection of our society. Therefore, this is a giant societal problem. But it must be dealt with.

First of all, the authorities, you see—to change the quality of authority, those in power must work on changing the quality of society as well. This goal must be set. Not simply to sit out one’s tenure in parliament or executive power. It is necessary to influence society, its enlightenment, its self-awareness, its creative potential. Therein lies the main task. Otherwise, you are right, it will drift on its own, like everything else.

Inal Khashig: It seems to me that the situation around the Abkhaz language is indeed much broader. It shows, probably, our attitude toward the law in general. This applies not only to the Abkhaz language.

We have passed very many all sorts of legislative acts, proper laws, but then we tried in every way to bypass them. An active advertising campaign is taking place on the internet: acquire Abkhaz real estate, and so forth. So many lances were broken over this law on apartments, and still they sell Abkhaz real estate to foreigners. It is possible, it can be acquired.

Astamur Tania: Yes, that is also—you know what the matter is? It is impossible to contain the onslaught; it can only be directed into some profitable channel. Of course, it is possible for some time to contain the natural course of events with prohibitions. But we must nevertheless forecast how we can direct these investments, where our weak zones are.

Simply sitting like a dog in the manger will not work. Therefore, we must understand how in this harsh reality—what is our place. Today one hole was plugged, in another place it tore open. We must have some clear program of action, at least for the short term.

This concerns the economy, security, foreign policy, everything. What I am saying is very banal, but unfortunately, we always have a reactive response to something, to already accomplished facts. Although it was not difficult to predict that the course of events was leading to this. And we live for today. If an individual person can live for today like that, the state should not live like that.

Inal Khashig: The state somehow manages to.

Astamur Tania: It should still plan its future, the society.

Inal Khashig: I would like to switch to another topic now. Periodically, we are reminded of the unresolved Georgian-Abkhaz conflict, which continuously remains at a dead end. Last time, we discussed how Georgian perceptions of Abkhazia and the Abkhaz people have changed, particularly through the influence of Pavel Ingorokva’s theory, which took a strong hold in Georgian thought.

Shortly after our conversation, I watched an interview with the Georgian historian Tsurtsumia on a Georgian YouTube channel. He noted that Ingorokva’s theory is actually marginal and lacks official state support.

Nevertheless, just the day before yesterday, I came across a vividly animated video. It was set in Sukhumi on the embankment, depicting peaceful civilians in a setting reminiscent of 1992, when a Russian military aircraft suddenly swoops in and begins bombing. The people are shown fleeing the embankment, trying to escape by ship or heading into the mountains.

Astamur Tania: Those are slightly different scenes, probably. Maybe it is one pie, but different slices.

Inal Khashig: Yes, but you see, this is proceeding very actively – why I understood this is not only Ingorokva’s theory about who the Abkhaz are and what their origin is, but in Georgian society the understanding of what the Georgian-Abkhaz conflict was is changing very actively. And what happened 33 years ago, 34 years ago. How the war started.

According to this cartoon… A cartoon is a certain part of upbringing. It also has its own audience. Directed at a certain audience. At children. It is important for me to understand why the Georgians converted this conflict into a conflict not between Georgians and Abkhaz, but a certain conflict between Russia and Georgia.

Astamur Tania: That is completely understandable, as acknowledging it would require admitting responsibility for starting the armed conflict. By the way, Shevardnadze did admit this responsibility—and while he claimed Kitovani was to blame, Kitovani was not the Defense Minister of Russia, but of Georgia. Everyone remembers, and archival footage still shows, how this war began and how the local Georgian population reacted.

Acknowledging this would require erasing entire sections of history. Instead, there is an effort to reshape the narrative of 1992 and merge it with the events of 2008, framing everything around legislation and the narrative of post-2008 occupation. Yet, a detailed examination—including the report by the International Fact-Finding Commission led by Heidi Tagliavini—confirmed that responsibility for initiating military action in both instances lay with the Georgian side.

Naturally, there is a desire to obscure this in the media space to advance narratives about occupation, aiming to shape international opinion to justify a forceful resolution or delegitimize the Abkhazian state.

We must react to this. The fact that animated videos are being produced on this topic shows an intent to pass this worldview down to the next generation. If we carry such a perspective into the future, achieving a peaceful settlement or joint progress will be extremely difficult. This is why it is essential to present the fullest possible picture, starting with the factual timeline.

Regarding Zura Tsurtsumia’s comments: first, it is positive that Georgian-Abkhaz relations are being examined at a solid academic level, attempting to move beyond today’s propaganda clichés toward a historical assessment of the conflict’s roots.

However, claiming that Ingorokva’s theory is marginal ignores reality in the Georgian media landscape, where it remains the most widespread view on the origins of the Abkhazian people. While prominent Georgian scholars considered it pseudoscientific—such as Javakhishvili, who noted that ancient Adyghe tribes inhabited Western Georgia prior to the Kartvelians and recognized the Apsilals and Abasgs as direct ancestors of modern Abkhaz—these classical works are largely ignored by mainstream media.

Instead, hate speech dominates the discourse among commentators—and we must acknowledge that hate speech exists on the Abkhaz side as well. Neither side benefits from this.

Objectively, neither we nor Georgia have any interest in a renewed armed conflict, which would yield disastrous consequences for both. Some in Georgian society may assume their larger population makes it an easy victory, but that is far from reality. We cannot afford to trigger such a dangerous cycle.

Both sides are equally served by abandoning hate speech and language that demeans human dignity and belittles culture, especially given that all human cultures, including Abkhazian and Georgian, are products of historical interaction and symbiosis.

Finally, addressing Tsurtsumia’s assertion—which is not unique to him—that the Abkhaz nation was deliberately engineered by Soviet authorities to counter Georgia: while Soviet policies influenced the development of both the Georgian and Abkhazian nations in the late 19th and 20th centuries, it is vital to recognize that the Abkhaz national identity was not an artificial creation.

In fact, during the 1930s and 1940s, deliberate repressive measures were used in an effort to suppress the formation of the Abkhaz nation.

Inal Khashig: That was when schools were closed.

Astamur Tania: Schools were closed, and the destruction of the intelligentsia—the bearers of this very idea—took place at that time. This inflicted a serious trauma.

But one must understand that this process is accomplished. It is an accomplished fact. And in dialogue with the Abkhaz, everyone must proceed from the premise that this is not simply an ethnos, but a formed nation. With its own ideas about borders, policy, with its own national mythology. This is not always equal to history. Here there is a completely different approach.

As I once spoke with an Abkhaz, he said in his heart: why did Gurandukht, the daughter of the Abkhaz king, marry Gurgen, the ruler of Tao-Klarjeti? Since then, the unification of the Abkhaz state with the Georgian one began. That is the feudal era. It is an accomplished fact. We can only look at it like that. It sounds like a parody.

The same applies to this issue. It is closer to us. These are already accomplished facts. We must take them into account. Proceed from the fact that this is a given. Second, there were in fact certain inaccuracies there.

I do not want to delve into that now. In itself, this attempt to approach the understanding of the origins of the Georgian-Abkhaz conflict with a cool head, using academic material—if this happens more or less regularly, in the same calm atmosphere, then it seems to me that both societies can win from this.

Inal Khashig: On the other hand, it seems to me, given that this seems to be a recent event—the war is relatively a historical event, only 30 years ago—nevertheless, judging by what I read in social networks, certain articles, certain speeches of politicians or experts…

Astamur Tania: Very much so.

Inal Khashig: I still see a lot of statements specifically adjusting to the political opportunism of the moment. If you remember, in the 80s, in the 90s after the war, what were we called? Abkhaz separatists. Now you practically do not hear this term.

Astamur Tania: By the way, they started calling us Abkhaz separatists back during the war, and before that—Gudauta separatists. Although during that period Abkhazia had not yet declared that it was ceasing any relations with Georgia and was not going to live with it within common borders.

In its time, on the initiative of Georgian figures, the process of all kinds of division began in Abkhazia. They separated the Georgian sector from the Abkhaz State University. Then they withdrew the football team. Then they withdrew the Georgian faction from the Supreme Council. They began to sit separately. That is, they apparently assumed that gradually they would somehow paralyze things. And here the question arises: who was the separatist?

And the same with this term. And, by the way, “Gudauta separatists”—later this very term migrated into the documents of the United Nations. And for some time after the end of the war, when our authorities were already located in Sukhumi, they continued to call us Gudauta separatists. I think for the Abzhua Abkhaz this is a bit offensive. Gudauta-Abzzua separatists would have been sound better.

Inal Khashig: But, nevertheless, this term somehow went out of circulation. And we have already been switched to the idea that Abkhazia is a territory occupied by Russia. And at the same time, as for the Abkhaz—let us leave aside those social networks where we generally came down from the mountains, according to the Georgian version—in official rhetoric nothing is said about us anymore.

Astamur Tania: “Came down from the mountains” is also quite amusing, because on most of the coast, based on climatic conditions and the unhealthiness of this climate, it was practically impossible to live permanently. Even if you open the press of, say, the late 19th and early 20th centuries, it is evident that the affluent portion of the residents of the city of Sukhumi left Sukhumi for the summer period. Precisely when there was the peak of this disease, people left for the foothills, because living here was a bit dangerous.

Inal Khashig: And the most prosperous ones lived there.

Astamur Tania: Generally, we have a perception as if in the Middle Ages communications in Abkhazia—this applies to everything, we are talking about Abkhazia—ran along the coast like that; there was the Ancient Roman railway running, next to it the Byzantine highway, but in reality all communications passed through the foothills and across the ridges. It was later, with the arrival of the Russian Empire, that this network of communications familiar to us began to develop. And psychologically we begin to tie our perception of the past to what had already taken shape in the 19th and 20th centuries. There was no railway at the beginning of the 20th century yet.

Inal Khashig: This highway that exists now.

Astamur Tania: For example, construction of the Black Sea railway continued in 1918 still. The Russian Empire no longer existed, but it was unclear what would happen. But they continued to build it in the Gagra region in 1918. And now it seems that it was always there.

Inal Khashig: But nevertheless, I tried to understand. Why do they depict Abkhaz who did not participate in this conflict, or played some secondary role in this Georgian-Abkhaz conflict? In the war that took place in 1992-1993.

Astamur Tania: A moment is omitted. What quantity of weapons was transferred to Georgia under the Tashkent Agreement on the eve of the conflict? The Russian authorities of that time were far from being, to put it mildly, pro-Abkhaz.

This is evident from everything. This is visible if one reads at least the transcript of September 3 of the meeting of Shevardnadze, Yeltsin, Ardzinba, representatives of the North Caucasus, representatives of our various parliamentary deputations. Not only should documents be studied, one should read the transcript.

But why did Georgia start armed conflicts? It received at its disposal several motor rifle and tank divisions of the Transcaucasus Military District. Therefore, in their joy, they thought that it would be possible to quickly finish this business.

Inal Khashig: But nevertheless, why am I saying all this—I read an interesting Georgian perspective on why this is happening, that Abkhaz are being excluded from this conflict, that through such an exclusion—and, say, when a certain image of the enemy is removed from the Abkhaz in this conflict, in this war, if the Abkhaz played a non-primary role, it means they are not enemies. There is a hypothetical possibility they retain that later at some point we will make peace with them.

Astamur Tania: That is very hypothetical. In my opinion, it is impossible to do that. Because how can one take a segment of a section of thinking and take something out of there… It seems to me this is very much a laboratory theory.

Inal Khashig: But this is laboratory on the one hand, and on the other hand the Abkhaz themselves have their own perception of the war.

Astamur Tania: To reiterate: those in Georgia who deal with the Georgian-Abkhaz settlement or seek to study this issue must start from the accomplished fact of the Abkhazian nation’s existence. A nation cannot be treated as a third-party observer—it is an active subject. We are an active subject in our relations with Georgia. Recognized or unrecognized, by our internal structure, we are a nation—with our own statehood and our own distinct perception of both the past and the future.

Our perspectives may not always align, but if we look at history honestly, our centuries-long—even thousand-year-old—relations with various Kartvelian peoples, primarily Megrelians, cannot simply be painted in black-and-white. History saw different periods, including feudal wars, which, it should be noted, occurred internally among those groups as well. There was continuous interaction, symbiosis, and movement back and forth. This is why we find Megrelian surnames in Abkhazia, Abkhaz surnames in Zugdidi, and why Gali in particular serves as a concentrated microcosm where everything is intertwined.

We, too, must draw important policy conclusions from this. But there must be a foundational understanding that if there is a real desire to settle our relations or develop a pragmatic approach—though I do not expect major breakthroughs given our disagreements—it starts with recognizing that a political nation has formed here. Its members are not solely ethnic Abkhazians, but all citizens of Abkhazia. We, too, must recognize this and move away from a narrow communal mindset.

Inal Khashig: But, by the way, it is present.

Astamur Tania: That is natural, because that is where it started. But we must nevertheless move in the direction of a civic nation.

Inal Khashig: Well yes, a political nation. This distinction is crucial because, unfortunately, many people’s perception of the Abkhazian situation and where we stand today was shaped back in Soviet times.

Astamur Tania: In fact, the post-Stalin Soviet period wasn’t all bad. Despite setbacks during that recovery process, it was unthinkable to express such vile ideas in writing back then.

Inal Khashig: My point is slightly different. In Soviet times, the Abkhaz struggle focused on ethnic rights—opening schools, theaters, literary journals, and universities—since few anticipated the collapse of the Soviet Union. The political nation back then was subsumed under the concept of the ‘Soviet people,’ right?

Astamur Tania: Well, ‘the Soviet people’ was an ideological construct, though autonomous frameworks did exist.

Inal Khashig: Yet today, some still take a fragmented approach, viewing society purely as separate ethnic groups—Abkhaz, Armenians, Russians, and so on—rather than…

Astamur Tania: You mean moving toward a unified civic nation?

Inal Khashig: Exactly. That is essential.

Astamur Tania: That requires active political education. Some processes occur naturally: living within the same state fosters shared views on security, peaceful development, and the necessity of an independent Abkhazia. However, we must establish clear criteria for this political nation to avoid repeating the mistakes made in Georgia during the Gamsakhurdia era. As a polyethnic society, we must embed protections that guarantee the survival of the Abkhaz people. Our fellow citizens understand this foundational principle.

That brings us back to language. Over time, our entire society must achieve sufficient command of the Abkhaz language for daily communication. Naturally, our society will remain bilingual due to demographic and geopolitical realities. This is why Russian is constitutionally designated alongside Abkhaz. But ‘alongside’ must not mean replacing Abkhaz. Striking this balance requires preserving the Abkhaz language while maintaining interethnic harmony. We should engage Abkhaz academic circles and draw on international experience—such as the major initiatives used to revive and preserve Welsh alongside English.

Ultimately, we need a sense of proportion in both domestic and foreign policy. Though emotions run high, avoiding extremes is vital. A population of our size can only survive through moderation and consensus.

Inal Khashig: Having come full circle, it seems clear that the survival and development of Abkhazia depend on building an inclusive civic nation that encompasses all ethnic groups residing here as citizens…

Astamur Tania: Including Georgians, of course.

Inal Khashig: …who would also command the state language.

Astamur Tania: Regarding the Gali district specifically, we must rethink our policy. We must acknowledge that regardless of how they identify ethnically, the residents there represent a native Megrelian-Georgian population, many with historical Abkhaz roots.

Inal Khashig: We can dedicate a separate conversation to that topic. But building a civic nation—governed by the rule of law and grounded in our constitutional language framework—is key to securing our future so that we aren’t constantly fearing our own disappearance.

Astamur Tania: Though I think we are destined to sound the alarm for many years to come!

Inal Khashig: Building a civic nation takes time and represents a broader movement toward a state governed by the rule of law.

Astamur Tania: To end on a reassuring note: perhaps artificial intelligence will solve all these problems for us!

Inal Khashig: I hope so! On that note, we will wrap up today’s broadcast. Today, Astamur Tania and I discussed the Abkhaz language, the Georgian-Abkhaz conflict, and why these complex questions persist. Goodbye. Until new meetings. Thank you.

Astamur Tania: Thank you.

The terminology, place names and views expressed in this article are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the editorial position of this website.

World.title: Breaking: SpaceX rocket splashes down off Christmas Island
World.content:
A large space rocket belonging to Elon Musk's SpaceX is being towed to the shores of Christmas Island after landing in the Indian Ocean, in an unusual spectacle for locals.

People on the remote Australian territory have lined up in droves along the rugged coastline to watch the rocket being towed by two large boats.

Christmas Island Tourism Association chair David Watchorn said it was "incredible" to see the spaceship up close.

"We'd heard some rumours that [SpaceX] might be coming to Christmas Island … and it was just there, huge," he said.

Two large ships tow in a piece of space debris off the coast of Christmas Island. (Instagram: @chrisbrayphotography)

"The boats out were super excited, you could see quite a number of vessels being launched off the boat around this morning to go and have a look."

Mr Watchorn said an exclusion zone was in place so vessels could not venture too close to the debris.

Hospitality owner Rachel Kucera said locals had flocked to her cafe today to see the space shuttle float past.

A rocket is being towed off Christmas Island, drawing crowds of locals to the coastline to catch a glimpse. (Supplied: David Watchorn)

"Everyone's been pretty fascinated by it I think, I don't think it's anything that we were ever expecting."

Christmas Island-based photographer Chris Bray, who usually focuses on wildlife, said the sight of the ships towing the rocket had become "the talk of the town".

A floating spaceship is seen in waters off Christmas Island on Tuesday. (Instagram: @chrisbrayphotography)

"At the moment it's just kind of hanging around off the sheltered side of the island and everyone's driving along to little vantage points to try and get a view of it," he said.

Recovery mission

US tech billionaire Musk's Starship Ship 40 was launched on July 24 from Texas, and after a successful mission re-entered the atmosphere and landed in the Indian Ocean far off the coast of Western Australia.

The Go Australis ship is next to suspected space junk in the waters off Christmas Island. (Supplied: David Watchorn)

Mr Musk publicly confirmed last week an effort was underway to retrieve it.

A spokesperson for the Australian Space Agency said the Australian government was coordinating with SpaceX to recover the Starship.

"SpaceX has towed the vehicle to Christmas Island after it re-entered and landed in international waters," the spokesperson said.

Elon Musk is the Chief Executive Officer of SpaceX and Tesla. (Reuters: Gonzalo Fuentes)

"Questions regarding Starship recovery operations and any future plans for Starship's return to the United States should be directed to SpaceX."

The company has been contacted for comment.

Space junk common

The space junk discovery off Christmas Island comes after a four-tonne abandoned upper stage of a Space X Rocket crashed into the moon two weeks ago, creating a visible crater and thrusting the issue into the public discourse.

Space archaeologist and Flinders University associate professor Alice Gorman said Australians should expect to see a lot more space junk over the next few years, given the surge in launches.

Loading...

"A study that was done a few years ago showed that as the number of launches increased, we specifically in the Southern Hemisphere are likely to get more space junk than the Northern Hemisphere is," she said.

" Australia has a very large land mass so things have a lot of space to land on; we also have a lot of coastline too. "

There have been several space junk incidents in Australia over the past few years.

Most recently, several metallic "space balls" were discovered on a north Queensland beach in July, which the Australian Space Agency confirmed were likely from a space launch vessel.

In October last year, space junk believed to be from a Chinese rocket was found near a mine site in Newman in WA's north.

Two years before that, space junk also washed up on a beach at Green Head, roughly 250 kilometres north of Perth.

Objects launched into space have skyrocketed in recent years, with 4,510 launches in 2025, compared to 586 in 2019, according United Nations Office for Outer Space Affairs data.

Most objects by far were launched by the United States, China was in second place, and Russia in third.

World.title: Construction worker confronted by men linked to bikie gang, CFMEU inquiry hears
World.content:
Three Melbourne men linked to the Comancheros bikie gang flew to Brisbane before one allegedly threatened a construction worker at a major government project, a commission of inquiry has heard.

Flight and phone records tendered to the probe into the CFMEU and construction sector revealed Bemir Saracevic, Krstomir Bjelogrlic and Mark Ahern arrived in Brisbane at around 11.20am on June 5, 2024.

Senior Counsel Assisting Eddy Gisonda KC told the inquiry the trio travelled to the Centenary Bridge upgrade site, where a crane operator said he was confronted around 12.30pm.

Mr Saracevic, known as Benji, was the former national president of the Comancheros, while Mr Bjelogrlic was his business partner. Mr Ahern was a former treasurer of the gang.

Senior Comancheros bikie Bemir 'Benji' Saracevic has been accused of threatening a CFMEU delegate during the union's dispute with a construction company on a major government-funded project in Brisbane. (Supplied)

Mr Gisonda said Gary Samuel, who ran security operator HOST at the construction site, had been on the phone and texting throughout the morning with senior management from contractor BMD, as well as Mr Saracevic.

Mr Samuel's phone also pinged near Brisbane Airport at about 11.50am.

"That's about the same time the three men are pinging data at the Brisbane Airport," he said.

"Do you want me to infer Mr Samuel picked those three men up and drove them to Centenary Bridge site," Commissioner Stuart Wood asked Mr Gisonda.

"Yes," he said in response.

Threats made towards crane operator

BMD had hired HOST to provide security on the site after ongoing CFMEU campaigns disrupted work on the project, the inquiry heard.

The crane operator on June 5, 2024 was Cody Raymond, a CFMEU delegate.

Key takeaways from the CFMEU inquiry in Queensland The inquiry heard accusations that police had failed to "enforce the law" during aggressive union disputes.

He is yet to give evidence to the inquiry, but in a workplace interview conducted eight days after the confrontation was tendered in evidence today.

Mr Raymond said he had been working in the crane when he noticed a group of four men "using strong hand gestures" near his colleague.

He said one of the men asked him "why the f*** are you threatening my men?"

"The man in the black shirt was attempting to be verbally intimidating. His questions were about an altercation I had with his acquaintance," he said.

That acquaintance, Mr Raymond alleges, was Gary Samuel.

"The man in the black shirt stated that I had 'threatened him and called him a goose'," he said.

Mr Raymond said the incident became more aggressive, with the man then saying "do you know who the f*** I am…. Benji, from the Commos".

"He responded with 'I'll f***en burn your house down c*** and kill your kids' brother … I f***en know where you live brother."

Mr Raymond said the incident did not make sense to him.

BMD General Manager Rob Pickard denied any knowledge of the incident prior to it happening.

He also denied Mr Samuel had told him the three Melbourne men were travelling to Brisbane to visit the project.

"[Mr Raymond] approached me [after the incident] and made a comment similar to what he said here, that he had just been accosted by a member of an outlaw motorcycle group," Mr Pickard told the inquiry.

"I said, hang on a minute, what are you talking about. He then went on to explain it a little bit more. I said we'd look into that."

BMD general manager Rob Pickard denied hearing any alleged threats. (Supplied)

Mr Pickard said he couldn't remember what he discussed with Mr Samuel in an early-morning phone call that day, nor could he recall seeing Mr Samuel at BMD's head office later that morning, before Mr Samuel travelled towards Brisbane Airport and then returned to the Centenary Bridge site.

Mr Pickard also denied signalling to traffic controllers and pointing at the bikie gang members when he was on site around the time of the incident.

CCTV showed to the inquiry placed Mr Pickard in the vicinity, with evidence suggesting he and another BMD manager walked ahead of the four men shortly before the confrontation.

Mr Pickard denied knowing what was about to occur or hearing the alleged threats.

The ABC is not alleging Mr Pickard has done anything wrong.

The inquiry continues in Brisbane tomorrow, with other senior leaders from BMD expected to give evidence.

World.title: Man on trial for allegedly raping teenage girl in Queensland town
World.content:
A man is on trial for allegedly raping a teenage girl he met while she was walking home from a house party in a Queensland country town.

Warning: This article contains details of alleged sexual assault some readers may find distressing.

Clay Benjamin Hall pleaded not guilty to two counts of rape at the beginning of his trial in Warwick District Court today.

The court was told Mr Hall met the girl, who was in her late teens at the time, on a street in Warwick, about 160 kilometres west of Brisbane, and allegedly raped her after she offered to show him a shortcut to the local showgrounds in the early hours of October 31, 2021.

Crown prosecutor Samantha O'Rourke told a jury of six women and six men that the girl had been at a house party earlier that night.

"As she walked home in the early hours of the following morning, alone and vulnerable, she was raped by a man who was a stranger to her," Ms O'Rourke said in her opening statement.

Hall described as 'cowboy'

Ms O'Rourke told the court Mr Hall and the girl talked briefly before he introduced himself and told her he was in town for the rodeo.

"She describes him as a cowboy," Ms O'Rourke said.

The jury heard that Mr Hall explained that he was trying to get to the local showgrounds and the girl offered to show him a shortcut.

Crown prosecutor Samantha O'Rourke outside the Warwick courthouse. (ABC Southern Qld: Grace Nakamura)

Ms O'Rourke said Mr Hall sexually propositioned the girl before allegedly raping her against a tree both vaginally and anally.

She said the girl later called her boxing instructor, who took her to the Warwick Base Hospital, where the police were called.

Defence barrister David Jones KC said it was not contested that Mr Hall had sex with the girl.

"The issue is consent," Mr Jones said.

Mr Jones told the jury to pay attention to the way the girl presented to police and said a "potential issue" was that she had been at a house party earlier in the night with people she did not know who were giving her drinks.

The trial will continue this week. (ABC Southern Qld: Grace Nakamura)

Mr Jones told the jury to consider whether it was possible the complainant was impacted by alcohol or "whether there was something else on her mind beyond liquor that makes it unreliable as to what occurred".

He said the girl had told her boxing instructor on the phone that she had found herself in a "bad situation" at the house party.

The trial before Justice Philip McCarthy KC is expected to continue tomorrow.

World.title: Lawyer for rapist Ralph Carr urges court to halt case
World.content:
Prosecutors have called on a County Court judge not to delay sentencing rapist celebrity agent Ralph Carr after his defence team made a rare legal move to halt the case.

Last month, a jury found Carr guilty of raping a woman at his West Melbourne home three years ago, an allegation he denied. A longstanding suppression order was also lifted, identifying Carr.

The complainant was the key witness in the case, and gave evidence in front of the jury for at least five days.

Today, defence barrister Dermot Dann KC argued that the judge, Frank Gucciardo, should postpone plans to sentence Carr next week.

The move, known as a "stay", would open the door for Carr to apply for bail ahead of a legal challenge in the Court of Appeal.

Dermot Dann (front) told the court the guilty verdicts against Ralph Carr (left) were a miscarriage of justice. (ABC News)

Mr Dann said it was the first time in 35 years he had made such an application, and described the jury verdict as "the most obvious miscarriage of justice I've ever seen".

"Anyone who was in court who saw and heard the complainant give evidence in this trial should be very, very concerned; very, very uncomfortable about the guilty verdicts," he said.

Mr Dann said anyone who was comfortable with the verdicts had "lost sight of what justice is".

However, prosecutor Matthew Fisher accused Mr Dann of making a "political and emotional" speech that was inappropriate and questioned whether it was designed to attract media attention.

Mr Fisher said the jury was aware of "issues" with some aspects of the complainant's evidence, but still decided beyond reasonable doubt that she was raped by Carr.

"Your honour should not entertain the stay application," he said.

Ronald Ryan is seen here between two police officers during his murder trial for murder. (ABC Archives)

In calling for a stay of sentence, Mr Dann referenced the cases of Robert Tait and Ronald Ryan, two men sentenced to hanging in Victoria in the 60s.

Tait's death sentence was eventually stayed, but Ryan's was not, making him the final man to be hanged in Australia.

Judge Gucciardo told Mr Dann his client was not the first person found guilty to proclaim their innocence and said it was not his task to re-assess the evidence considered by the jury.

"What we had was a very conscientious jury who listened to the evidence, who listened to your very complete and, may I say, exceptional cross-examination of the complainant," the judge said.

" The whole process was exactly as it should have been. "

In scenes that resembled a mock appeal, Mr Dann outlined 16 pieces of evidence the defence was challenging, pointing to alleged inconsistencies with the woman's account of the night in question and other events.

Ralph Carr appeared in the pre-sentence hearing without his trademark black wig. (ABC News)

Carr began crying in the court dock as Mr Dann described his mental health issues and history of suicide attempts.

Yesterday, he said Carr was in "a living hell" while in an isolated prison cell for 23 hours a day.

However, Mr Fisher, for the prosecution, said the court should be "circumspect" when considering evidence from Carr's psychiatrist about his mental health.

"There's a great deal of speculation about how things might eventuate if the accused man remains in custody for a significant period of time," he said.

Prosecutors are expected to address the judge further about the nature of Carr's offending and the impact on the victim tomorrow.

If the judge refuses Carr's stay application, he is likely to be sentenced next Thursday.

He could spend months in jail before the case is brought before Victoria's Court of Appeal.

World.title: What you need to know about the working holiday visa pause
World.content:
The federal government has paused visa applications for working holiday-makers from 24 countries.

The temporary visa provides access to young people from overseas to fill labour shortages while travelling in Australia.

Here is what we know about the pause and countries affected, as experts weigh-in on the impact on industries that rely on these visa holders.

What is a working holiday-maker visa?

It is still unclear why working holiday visa applications have been paused from the two dozen countries. (Flickr: Slim Teller)

The Working Holiday Maker (WHM) program started in 1975 and was launched to promote cultural exchange between young people from Australia and around the world.

It started with an uncapped visa stream known as the 417 subclass, which now has 19 partner countries including Canada, France, Japan and the United Kingdom.

Decades later a separate capped WHM visa stream, known as subclass 462, began and now includes 29 countries.

Indonesia, China and the US were the top three citizenship countries of subclass 462 visas in the six-month period to June 30, last year, according to the Department of Home Affairs.

As of June 30, 2025 there were 206,187 working holiday-makers in Australia.

What does a 'pause' mean?

At a press conference in Sydney on Sunday, Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke said the WHM visas were "being processed more slowly than they were previously".

He did not comment further on the changes.

On the website for the Work and Holiday visa subclass 462, applications for visas from 24 countries have been paused.

The website says applications are temporarily paused when the cap is nearly filled or to spread out visa applications lodgements throughout the program year.

"Lodgements may also be paused to support the Government's migration settings while ensuring the program operates sustainably," the page reads.

Tony Burke says the WHM visas were "being processed more slowly than they were previously". (ABC News: Matt Roberts)

Immigration lawyer Chris Johnston, who has worked in the industry for decades, said the government's actions were "dramatic".

"I do believe [in the past], they have paused, or run out of allocations, so these sort of things have happened before," Mr Johnston told ABC.

" But when you look at the screen, [almost] the whole screen is blue [paused]. So this is different to one country running out of allocations, or a one-off pause. "

Applications from 24 countries have been paused according to the Department of Home Affairs website. (Department of Home Affairs)

He also said the changes were not officially announced.

"It was just something that was put up on the website of the Department of Home Affairs," he said.

"It was quietly put out there."

Which countries are affected?

Applications from almost all of the 29 countries that are part of the capped working holiday-maker visa stream have been paused.

It includes countries with higher caps, such as Indonesia, Spain, Argentina and Singapore.

Indonesia, which has an annual allocation of 5,000 places for working holiday-maker applicants, is among the countries subject to the pause. (Reuters: Willy Kurniawan)

Applications are still being accepted from five countries.

San Marino and Türkiye have 100 places each — on a first in, first served basis — while China, India and Vietnam operate on a ballot system.

Countries facing WHV application pause Argentina

Austria

Brazil

Chile

Czech Republic

Ecuador

Greece

Hungary

Indonesia

Israel

Luxembourg

Malaysia

Mongolia

Papua New Guinea

Peru

Poland

Portugal

Singapore

Slovak Republic

Slovenia

Spain

Switzerland

Thailand

Uruguay Source: Department of Home Affairs

Why are the visa applications paused?

It is still unclear why applications have been paused, but experts say it might have to do with a broader discussion about net overseas migration, or NOM.

"Many visa programs are suffering, either through slow processing, there's a high number of refusals for student visas, and now we can see that attention is also being turned to working holiday visas," Mr Johnston said.

According to the Australian Bureau of Statistics, NOM is the number of incoming migrant arrivals minus outgoing migrant departures over a specific period.

The Labor government aims to cut net migration to 225,000 people annually. (AAP: Bianca de Marchi)

If the government's objective was to reduce net overseas migration, Abul Rizvi, a former deputy secretary of the Department of Immigration, said "slow processing is a very, very poor way to do it".

"Slow processing usually just creates more problems than it solves," he said.

"It's a short-term solution to a long-term problem."

WHV holders have the option to extend their visas for up to three years and Mr Rizvi said removing the final year, that was introduced during the COVID pandemic, would be a "sensible" move from a net migration perspective.

In a statement to the ABC, the Department of Home Affairs did not specifically address the pause.

"Reforms to the Working Holiday Maker (WHM) program will better control demand and provide a fairer allocation of WHM visas," a department spokesperson said.

How does this impact visa applicants?

Wendi Aylward, a spokesperson for the Backpacker and Youth Tourism panel (BYTAP), said the industry received "very little information" from the government.

"Those who had applied under the 417 or 462 visa after July 1, anyone who's contacted Immigration to try and get an update on their visa have just been told that they need to wait," she said.

"And remember we're now in mid-August, so we have people that applied in early July and are still waiting."

Wendi Aylward from the Backpacker and Youth Tourism panel says the organisation has received minimal information on the visa pause. (Supplied)

Mr Johnston said the pause would be a "big problem" for applicants who had not lodged their application.

"The pause basically means they will not be able to lodge a new one whilst it's paused … so they will have to change their plans and wait until it opens again," he said.

"But when it opens, it might not be as easy to get as it previously was."

Mr Rizvi said the slowdown would be "quite unfair" for applicants.

"A pause or a slowdown just means the backlog of applications builds up," he said.

"All those applicants would be legally valid applications and would have to be processed, so you haven't actually solved any problem."

How does it impact Australia?

Ms Aylward said working holiday-maker visa holders play an "important" role in regional Australia, especially in the horticulture industry.

"Those farmers [in regional areas] may need someone only for a week or a couple of days, and that's where a working holiday-maker becomes just so critical," she said.

"They are regionally dispersed, and the wonderful thing is they spend the money that they make in those communities."

Mr Burke said the Pacific Workers Scheme was the "principal visa for the agricultural industry". (Supplied: Backpacker and Youth Tourism Panel)

In 2019, working holiday-makers contributed $3.2 billion to the Australian economy, according to Tourism Australia.

The tourism body reported at least $726 million of that was spent in regional areas.

Ms Aylward said there was concern about what the pause would mean for the tourism sector.

"Working holiday-makers create jobs in regional Australia because they use the travel operators, they go to the bakeries, they stay at the hostels," she said.

"So, they not only do the work themselves, but they facilitate and create employment in Australia."

NSW modern slavery report NSW parliamentary inquiry finds evidence of migrant workers living in near uninhabitable conditions, forced to work demanding hours and threatened if they spoke up.

When questioned on the impact of the visa processing for the agricultural industry, Mr Burke said the Pacific Workers Scheme or PALM was the "principal visa for the agricultural industry".

Mr Rizvi said that answer surprised him given the "massive levels of exploitation and abuse" that were detailed in a report on that scheme from a NSW parliamentary inquiry.

"I'm surprised the government is encouraging people to apply for the Pacific visa that has so many different problems," he said.

World.title: WA Police appeal for help to find missing 10-year-old girl
World.content:
Western Australian police are searching for a 10-year-old girl who has been missing from Perth for three days.

Lyndel Ningella was last seen in the northern suburb of Butler around 6pm on Saturday, August 15.

It is believed she was wearing a black jumper and black shorts and may have travelled to the suburbs of Kwinana, Leda, Parmelia or Wellard.

Assistant Superintendent Darren Hart said police were concerned for her safety.

"We hold concerns for Lyndel due to her young age and believe she may be staying with family and associates," he told reporters.

Assistant Superintendent Darren Hart said police were concerned for her safety. (ABC News: Pip Waller)

"It's believed she may have travelled to the Wellard area, in the Mandurah police district and was possibly there across the weekend.

"We are concerned for her safety in that she is a 10-year-old girl who is making her own way in the world."

Lyndel is described as being about 160 centimetres tall with a medium build, brown eyes and long brown hair with blonde ends.

Anyone who sees Lyndel or has information on her whereabouts is urged to contact police immediately.

World.title: Family of missing 18yo hiker confronts 'unimaginable situation'
World.content:
The family of missing bushwalker Lily Hooper is dealing with an "unimaginable situation" as the search for the 18-year-old continues.

Ms Hooper left her home south-west of Sydney last Wednesday morning to go hiking in the Nattai National Park in the Southern Highlands.

Her car was later found near the Bonnum Pic Walking Trail, but despite an extensive multi-agency operation beginning on Wednesday night, there has been no trace of the experienced bushwalker.

Efforts to find Lily Hooper have continued on day seven. (ABC Illawarra: Brooke Chandler)

'Beloved daughter'

The family released a statement through NSW Police today.

"Our family is absolutely devastated that our beloved daughter Lily is missing," the family said.

"We would like to thank all the emergency services and volunteers for their support and continued commitment to the search, not only during the day but throughout the night."

They wrote that they were "desperate" to bring Lily home safe and asked the community to keep the family and Lily in their thoughts.

"We appreciate people who have made offers for the search, but due to the terrain and conditions we ask just professional search teams continue," the family wrote in the statement.

" We also ask for privacy and understanding as our family navigates this unimaginable situation. "

Search continues

The search is now in its seventh day today, but authorities said they had not given up hope of finding the experienced bushwalker.

Search teams from multiple agencies were on the ground today. (ABC Illawarra: Brooke Chandler)

Specialist police crews were joined by 200 teams from the SES and rescue helicopters at the command site today, where they have been taking turns to work through the trail day and night.

Crews scoured dense bush, deep ravines and clifftops in their search and have battled inclement weather, which is expected to clear on Thursday.

NSW Police said there had been no trace of Ms Hooper or her belongings, and that her family was assisting in the search effort.

Search teams have battled extremely difficult terrain during the search. (Supplied: VRA NSW)

The terrain has been described as "incredibly rough", vast and dense, complicating efforts to cover the search area.

Police previously said they were unable to determine Ms Hooper's intended route beyond the Bonnum Pic Walking Trail, and whether she reached a nearby peak.

They previously said they believed Ms Hooper had her mobile phone with her and they were continuing to examine telecommunications information that could help establish where she went after arriving at the national park.

World.title: Photos of bedside rifle cartridges shown to Bogie triple murder trial
World.content:
The trial of a Queensland cattle farmer, accused of murdering the owners of a neighbouring property, has viewed photos of rifle cartridge packets found inside his home.

Prosecutors have told a Supreme Court trial being held in Townsville that spent shell casings with "30.30 WIN RP" markings were found around the bodies of married couple Mervyn Schwarz and Maree Schwarz and Mrs Schwarz's son Graham Tighe.

Maree Schwarz (left), Mervyn Schwarz and Graham Tighe (right) were found dead outside the gate of a Bogie cattle station in 2022. (Supplied/ABC News)

The jury heard the trio were found fatally wounded outside the gate of Darryl Valroy Young's Bogie cattle station on August 4, 2022.

Mr Young, who was charged over their deaths, has pleaded not guilty to three counts of murder.

He has also pleaded not guilty to the attempted murder of Ross Tighe, who earlier told the trial he was shot by Mr Young, and saw the farmer shoot dead his family.

Photographs taken by police investigators and presented to the trial today showed two packets of cartridges for a .30-30 calibre rifle.

The court heard the packets were found inside Mr Young's home, beside medication prescribed to him, next to a bed.

Monique Sheppard tendered photos of .30-30 rifle cartridges today. (ABC News: Baz Ruddick)

Crown prosecutor Monique Sheppard presented the photos taken by Queensland Police Senior Constable Kerrod Vaughn and noted the absence of cartridges inside one of the packets.

"There seems to be five cartridges absent.

"That is correct," Senior Constable Vaughn replied.

The trial has heard that Mr Young was not licensed to carry a .30-30 calibre rifle and that no such weapon was found on his property, Shannonvale Station.

Mr Young's neighbour, Brett Stagg, earlier told the trial that he once owned a .30-30 calibre rifle but that it went missing during a fire at his property in 2011.

Darryl Young has taken notes throughout the trial. (ABC News: Carole Howlett)

Disconnected cameras

The trial has also viewed photos of trail cameras and dozens of memory cards inside Mr Young's kitchen, after Ross Tighe said cameras usually at the gate of Shannonvale Station were missing on the day of the alleged murders.

Ross Tighe was the first witness the crown called to give evidence in the trial of Darryl Valroy Young. (ABC News: Carole Howlett)

Photos of the bloodstained Land Cruiser driver's seat, where Mrs Schwarz was found dead, were also presented to the jury today.

Ms Sheppard tendered several photos of a small circular hole that could be seen in the damaged window of the driver-side door.

Photos of shell casings around the bodies of Mr Schwarz and Graham Tighe, who lay outside the Land Cruiser, were also presented to the jury yesterday.

Stepmother refused statement

The trial heard Mr Young was arrested late on August 4, 2022 alongside his son, Derek Young, and his stepmother, Sharon Young, as well as two wind-farm workers, but that only Mr Young was accused of wrongdoing.

His lawyer, Anthony J Kimmins, told the trial Mr Young never saw the Schwarzes or the Tighes on the day he is accused of shooting them.

Police revealed yesterday that Sharon Young refused repeated requests from detectives to give a statement in the days after the alleged shooting.

The trial has heard that Derek Young, who gave evidence last week, did provide police with a statement.

Derek Young told the trial he saw his father talking to Sharon Young after Darryl Young had returned from the station gate on the morning of August 4, 2022.

He said his father and Sharon Young also travelled together in an all-terrain vehicle later that day to meet with wind-farm workers installing equipment at the property.

The trial continues.

World.title: Ralph Carr vows to fight for his freedom as lawyer rebuked over ‘emotional’ speech
World.content:
NationalVictoriaCourts Ralph Carr vows to fight for his freedom as lawyer rebuked over ‘emotional’ speech Erin Pearson August 18, 2026 — 6:38pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Sports and entertainment manager Ralph Carr plans to fight for his freedom for as long as it takes, a court has heard as his lawyer branded Carr’s rape conviction the most obvious miscarriage of justice he had seen in a decades-long career. But Dermot Dann’s strong defence of his client was met by tense debate from the judge and from the prosecutor, who accused the King’s Counsel of making inappropriate political and emotional statements. A court sketch of Ralph Carr. Paul Tyquin The second day of Carr’s pre-sentence hearing was underscored by both sides trading legal blows amid looks of frustration, eye rolling and whispering throughout hours of legal argument over his application to stay the case pending an appeal. Carr, who once counted Brownlow medallist Dustin Martin as a client and business partner and was married to singer Tina Arena, was found guilty last month of two counts of rape and one of sexual assault, following a jury trial in the County Court. He maintains his innocence.



On Tuesday, lawyers for the 66-year-old argued there had been a serious miscarriage of justice and the jury verdict was unsafe. Related Article Courts Entertainment stalwart Ralph Carr identified as mystery rapist after suppression order lifted Dann acknowledged his application to stay the case was a rare legal move only to be used in the most exceptional circumstances. “We submit that anyone who was in this court … and saw and heard the complainant give evidence in this trial should be very, very concerned and very, very uncomfortable about the guilty verdicts,” he said. “There should be no one who feels comfortable with those verdicts, and anyone who does ... has lost sight of what justice is and justice means.”



Dann said that in his 35 years of experience, Carr’s case was the most obvious miscarriage of justice he had seen. But Judge Frank Gucciardo told Dann his client would not be the first convicted man to claim his innocence and that it was inappropriate to overstate claims and express personal views at that point of the hearing. “I respectfully differ,” Dann replied. Gucciardo said he was not troubled by the jury verdicts and would not reassess the evidence. He said the jurors were conscientious, engaged by the evidence and cross-examination, and took copious notes before days of deliberations. “The whole process seemed to be exactly how it should’ve been. It seems to me you’ve got the hurdle to jump,” the trial judge said.



In carving out the issues for the defence, Dann said the complainant’s evidence changed during her six days in the witness box compared with what she had previously told police. Dustin Martin poses with Carr, then the footballer’s manager, after winning the 2017 Brownlow Medal. Getty Images Differences, he said, included the length of the alleged rapes and whether Carr was clothed or partially undressed. Dann also maintained the complainant had a financial motive to lie, pointing to a pending civil case. A future appeal, he said, had good prospects, and he pointed to his client’s declining mental health and placement in solitary confinement as reasons for his possible release on bail if the stay application was granted. Prosecutor Matthew Fisher said he had serious concerns about how Dann was referring to Carr’s plight and any potential miscarriage of justice.



“We are very concerned on this side of the Bar table. To make a political or emotional speech to your honour … is entirely inappropriate,” Fisher said. Related Article Courts ‘Like a living hell’: Rapist Ralph Carr unrecognisable in court appearance “We hope he hasn’t made that statement to your honour to garner or attract some sort of media attention to his client’s cause. It was open to the jury to reach the verdicts that they did.” The court heard the woman had elected not to read or compile a victim impact statement for the court. Her evidence during the trial was held in closed court. Carr was found guilty in July after the jury heard he and the victim had been consuming alcohol and cocaine at his home in 2023 when he raped her.



His identity was suppressed for three years after his legal team obtained a suppression order to conceal his alleged involvement in the assault citing mental health concerns. On Monday, the court heard Carr was confined to his prison cell for 23 hours a day, and believes the verdict has destroyed his career. Dann said his client’s declining mental health warranted mitigation of his sentencing along with Carr’s lack of criminal history, prior good character, and the significant contribution he had made to the community. The pre-sentence hearing and stay application will continue on Wednesday. If you or anyone you know needs support, you can contact the National Sexual Assault, Domestic and Family Violence Counselling Service on 1800RESPECT (1800 737 732), Lifeline 131 114, or Beyond Blue 1300 224 636. World.title: Minister denies eye roll at veterans pleading for healthcare funding
World.content:
PoliticsFederalPolitical leadership Minister denies eye roll at veterans pleading for healthcare funding Brittany Busch August 18, 2026 — 6:33pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Veterans’ Affairs Minister Matt Keogh has conceded he made a mistake by refusing to meet former defence personnel who are calling for Labor to scrap a cap on allied health service funding, but denied accusations he rolled his eyes at the veterans and refused to shake their hands. The Coalition of Veterans’ Voices is in Canberra this week urging the government to abandon an annual $5000 cap on allied health services for veterans, introduced in the May budget and set to start next year. Minister for Veterans’ Affairs Matt Keogh during question time on Tuesday. Dominic Lorrimer Keogh met the advocacy group on Monday after the Coalition launched a scathing attack on the minister. The allied health services cap has further strained the minister’s relationship with the veteran community after he abandoned plans to scrap funding for the Invictus Games and pull travel assistance funding for the parents of Victoria Cross recipient Cameron Baird. Former pilot Dr Tim Nelson said he had no faith in the department’s ability to administer the cap and accused Keogh of rolling his eyes during Monday’s meeting.



Related Article City life The knock on the door: 57 years on, a Vietnam War widow tells her story “It was obvious he did not want to be there,” Nelson told a press conference in Canberra on Tuesday. “He walked into the room, refused to shake our hand, sat down with his arms crossed, and rolled his eyes.” Former navy clearance diver John Armfield, whose brother died by suicide, said Keogh was too focused on the budget bottom line. “Minister Keogh forgets he was elected to serve, not self-serve,” Armfield said. “The budget’s obviously playing a role here. He wants the savings to go with that.” Labor identified the $6.6 billion veterans fund as a target for savings in May, and Finance Minister Katy Gallagher likened it to the NDIS because dodgy doctors were skimming payments meant for retired defence personnel. The budget measures aim to claw back more than $700 million over four years.



Veterans with critical needs can apply for greater funding for services, including occupational therapists, physiotherapists and psychologists once they reach the cap, which Labor says is necessary to prevent overcharging. But veterans have argued that it creates an extra hurdle for those in crisis. Keogh said on Tuesday he had made a mistake for not agreeing to meet the veterans in the first instance, but rejected Nelson’s characterisation of his behaviour in the meeting. “I acknowledge that I got it wrong not agreeing to meet with them last week when that initial request came,” he said. “When I came into that room, I met with them, and they were sitting down. I said, ‘Relax, and I want to hear what you want to tell me’ … and I shook the hands of those people who attended that meeting as we finished that meeting, to be clear.” Keogh acknowledged the distrust of the department within the veteran community, and said a discussion paper to consult on the changes would be released soon.



He has argued Labor is making it easier for veterans to access allied health services by committing nearly $170 million to increasing fees for providers that had been threatening to cut back services, and said the government was striving to ensure veterans did not pay a gap fee. Opposition defence industry and personnel spokesman Phillip Thompson, himself a veteran, said the community Keogh represented had lost faith in his leadership. Thompson has attacked Keogh over the “cruel cuts”, referencing his own mental health struggles and warning that veterans were planning to take their own lives when they hit the annual cap because they swore to never be a burden on their families. Nationals leader Matt Canavan said allied health services saved lives, and called on the prime minister to meet those affected by the cap. “Those that do sacrifice for our nation don’t just leave scars on the battlefield. They are left with scars for life, and understandably, they need help … and support from professionals,” he said.

World.title: Labor’s controversial gambling bill will pass - with fresh headaches for the government
World.content:
Breaking PoliticsFederalGambling Labor’s controversial gambling bill will pass - with fresh headaches for the government Natassia Chrysanthos and Paul Sakkal Updated August 18, 2026 — 6:23pm ,first published 2:22pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Australians who don’t want to see gambling ads online will be able to opt out with a new “AdStop” regime but the government will be scrambling to design a workable scheme and deal with privacy concerns as its wagering laws become mired in complexity. Last-minute amendments will not block freebies for punters as former addicts and their families had hoped. A new rule stopping inducements for problem gamblers still needs a definition of high-risk customers to give it teeth, setting up a fresh fight with the gambling industry. Prime Minister Anthony Albanese puts the Gambling Reform Bill 2026 to the House of Representatives as Communications Minister Anika Wells looks on. Dominic Lorrimer The amendments were introduced on Tuesday in a compromise deal between Prime Minister Anthony Albanese and Angus Taylor. The opposition leader also signed off on Labor’s National Disability Insurance Scheme overhaul, which was due to pass the Senate on Tuesday night, in exchange for the government expediting moves to rid a “widow’s tax” from tax changes. Labor was forced to amend its gambling legislation after a Senate inquiry into the laws this month heard alarming testimony about addicts, including former NRL player Luke Bateman, being lured into wagering with drugs, escorts and thousands of dollars in free bets.



More than three years after the late Labor MP Peta Murphy’s bipartisan report recommended a total ban on gambling ads and inducements, the Labor caucus signed off on the changes. Albanese told MPs the government had struck a balance between protecting children and permitting Australia’s betting culture, and told parliament that the revised package was “the most significant gambling advertising reform by any Australian government ever”. Loading Some Labor MPs said the changes were a good start and could be strengthened over time, but several were downhearted. Others said the government’s late changes made the package so complex as to be unworkable. In a sign of discontent about the final bill and the fractious process leading up to it, some Liberal MPs yelled complaints in question time as the prime minister talked up the reform. Cook MP Simon Kennedy heckled Albanese about having been embarrassed into strengthening the bill.



All the independent crossbenchers, many of whom have campaigned for stronger gambling action, voted against the bill when it came to the House of Representatives on Tuesday night. “Only three hours of debate after three long years of waiting,” said Curtin MP Kate Chaney. “Trust in politics is eroded when the major parties do deals like this on legislation that are made for political convenience, not based on evidence.” They were joined by the Greens, Nationals MP Pat Conaghan and Liberal MP Andrew Wallace, who crossed the floor against Coalition policy for the first time in his 10-year parliamentary career, saying the amendments “don’t go anywhere near” fixing problem gambling. “I can’t in good conscience vote for [the bill],” Wallace said. Under the original package announced in April, viewers will see no more than three gambling ads per hour on television. There will also be a phased-in ad ban for stadiums and jerseys, a ban on sports stars promoting wagering, and tighter limits on radio ads in school pick-up hours. Online platforms will have to offer registered adult users the option of opting out of digital ads.



A further amendment applies the same hourly ad limit to television and online streaming services, after the Coalition pushed Labor to reverse its plans to give streaming services carte blanche if registered users didn’t opt out of watching gabling ads. Viewers won’t see gambling ads for 15 minutes before a game – an extension from the previously planned five minutes – and hourly ad limit will start an hour earlier, at 5am. The laws will have to be reviewed in three years and betting companies will be levied to pay for compliance of the online advertising opt-out regime. Betting inducements Opposition communication spokeswoman Sarah Henderson said the Coalition was “very pleased to have prosecuted these amendments in the best interests of all Australians”.



“We heard some damning evidence, including from the likes of Mr Bateman, so this, for the first time, combats predatory inducements,” she said. But the new rules for betting inducements – which include free bonus bets and the services of VIP agents – dismayed advocates who wanted an all-out ban, recommended by the Murphy report. Related Article Gambling ‘I can’t stop to save my own life’: Parents read son’s final plea on gambling addiction In addition to banning inducements for risky gamblers, gambling companies will have to wait 14 days after someone opens an account to offer them any promotions. There will be a 90-day wait time for people attempting to move off the self-exclusion platform BetStop. Reform advocates argue the industry cannot be trusted, given evidence to the Senate inquiry about problem gamblers lured with free bets. One person was offered $50,000 in free bets despite losing about $500,000 in a month.



The government will move to define high-risk gamblers in law, sources said. But the threshold has not been determined. It could gauge someone’s betting frequency, for example, or how much money had been drained from their bank account. Given promotions represent about 30 per cent of turnover for the racing industry, this will set up a fresh fight between the government and gambling sector, which will push officials to adopt existing thresholds already used in some states and territories. Independent MP Allegra Spender said either way the law would not intervene until people had already become problem gamblers. “We are literally providing the pathway ... for people’s lives to be ruined by gambling, and then say: ‘Oh, by the time that you get there, we’ll see if we can do anything to make this a little bit easier for you’,” she said. “The government has an option. The opposition has an option. It could just go out there and ban inducements altogether ... It is deeply disappointing to all the people who came and gave their time and effort to all the inquiries.



“Because we could be making Australians safer right now, and we have chosen not to, and that is a decision that has been made by the major parties.” Advertising opt-out The other amendment that will create a technical headache for the government is the opt-out regime. This was another push from the Coalition, concerned that people would be reluctant to opt out of advertising across all their online accounts. The “AdStop” scheme will be administered by the Australian Communications and Media Authority, using funding from a levy to be imposed on gambling companies.



Government sources said it could involve people nominating either their email address or mobile phone number to the ACMA register. Online platforms would then have to reconcile their customer details with the register and would not be allowed to show gambling ads to registered accounts. This would apply to online streaming services as well as social media accounts. But the register won’t be ready when the new advertising rules come into force on January 1, given it will require time to work out and likely raise privacy concerns. The peak body representing firms such as Sportsbet, Responsible Wagering Australia, said the AdStop proposal was unwieldy. “Betstop, which is a simpler concept, took more than four years from inception to implementation,” the outfit’s chief executive, Kai Cantwell, said.

World.title: Why the selectors’ SOS to Renshaw is 10 years in the making
World.content:
Updated SportCricketAustralian cricket Why the selectors’ SOS to Renshaw is 10 years in the making Daniel Brettig Updated August 18, 2026 — 6:18pm ,first published 12:52pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Townsville: Nearly a decade has passed since a 21-year-old Matt Renshaw was dropped from the Australian Test team with an average of 36.64 from 10 matches. Save for Usman Khawaja (48.05), Travis Head (53.77) and David Warner (40.91), no one since has performed anywhere near as well in the opening role. Jake Weatherald became the latest casualty on Tuesday after he was dropped not only from the team but the squad entirely to make way for Renshaw’s return. Only a few months have passed since Weatherald beat Renshaw to a Cricket Australia contract for this season, but the former’s struggles in Darwin were so acute across two innings that the selectors chose to make a clean break. It is difficult now to see Weatherald making the October tour of South Africa. Matthew Renshaw (left) will replace Jake Weatherald (right) at the top of Australia’s batting order in the Mackay Test match against Bangladesh. Getty In addition to making two low scores in Darwin in the First Test, Weatherald looked jumpy and uneasy at the batting crease, having admitted that his fate would be out of his hands if he didn’t make a score in his hometown.



“You are required to make runs all the time when you’re out there, and I’ve got a good opportunity to play two games hopefully and make some runs,” Weatherald had said. “If I don’t do that, then, yeah, I put my fate in someone else’s hands and I haven’t done enough. "It's a challenge when people you respect say things about your batting, or your game. You're naturally always looking for affirmation, and people to respect what you're doing, but at the same time it's a part of cricket. “I understand now it’s just a part of the game I’m playing, but it’s a great challenge as well. That’s what makes Test cricket so hard – you’re in the spotlight, you need to do a lot of things, not just make runs. If you can do it all, it makes for a good career.” Loading Renshaw made his Test debut in Adelaide a decade ago and was harshly left out of the team the following year when he was replaced by Cameron Bancroft. Ironically, Renshaw’s last Tests in that initial stint with the team were in Australia’s previous series against Bangladesh in 2017.



Then-selection chair Trevor Hohns had suggested Renshaw would ultimately be a long-term player for Australia, but it has been a long and frustrating road back. “The way Matthew is playing at the moment – we don’t consider it ideal to inject him into the first Test versus England,” Hohns said in 2017. “Matthew is highly regarded by us a selection panel, and we certainly see him as a long-term player for Australia. We’d ideally like him to go back to Sheffield Shield cricket, re-evaluate the way he’s playing and belt the door down with runs and demand selection.” Back then, there was a view that Renshaw was talented but lacking maturity, something that still seemed to be an issue when he was subjected to some hard training sessions and then swiftly discarded by then coach Justin Langer after a 2018 tour of the UAE.



Now married and a father, Renshaw has made sporadic appearances since while honing his game, but in recent times has been a consistent presence in white-ball squads and was the best-performing batter on the recent limited-overs tour of Bangladesh where the hosts beat Australia in the ODI series. More recently, Renshaw was part of the extended 19-man training squad in Brisbane ahead of the Darwin Test. Skipper Pat Cummins had alluded to the likelihood of a batting change after the nine-wicket loss to Bangladesh. “I think it’s a balance of it’s one Test, but it’s also a bit of a trend as well, so [we’re] trying to work out do you need to intervene now, or let it play out, and you think it’s the way forward,” Cummins said. “That’s the question over the next couple of days – we’ll sit down and have a think, selectors will have a think, is there something there that’s going to take us forward, or is it starting to become a trend that we think needs to be changed? “It’s pretty clear it’s not quite functioning as well as we’d like as a group, so I’m sure the batters will get together and talk – review some footage, review methods, their approaches to how they were this week. If we need to make some changes to our style, we’ve got a week or so and we better do it pretty quickly.”



Related Article Australian cricket ‘He needs big runs’: Blowtorch on Marnus as selectors hear growing calls for change Former Test opener and fellow Queenslander Matthew Hayden has been an outspoken advocate for Renshaw’s return to the top of the Test batting order. “I want some experience at the top,” Hayden said on Seven. “I want to see Matt Renshaw, and I’ve been saying this for at least 12 months. I think he is match-fit … I think the selectors knew what he was, [and] now I want to see what he actually is.” Unlike Weatherald, who was very visible in marketing for the Darwin Test, Renshaw is expected to keep a low profile before Saturday’s first ball as he reconnects with Test cricket.
